A SONG BY A CONTENTED FELLOW. Oh, 'tie all one to me, all one, Whether I've money or whether ce none. He who has money can buy him a wife, And he who has none can be free for life. He who has money can trade if he choose, And he who has none has nothing to lose. Ile who has money has cares not a few, And he who has none can alef p the night through. He who has money can squint at the fair, And he who has none escapes with much care. He who has money can go to the play, And he who has none at home can stay. He who has money can travel about, And he who has none can do without. He who has money can be coarse as he will, And he who has none can be coarser still. He who has money can drink the best wine,• And he who has none with the gout will net pine. He v•ho has money the cash must pay, And he who has none says, "Charge it, I pray." He who has money must die some day, And he who has none must go the same way. Oh, 'tis all one to me, all one, Whether I've money or whether I've none.

-- A vigilant sentinel is posted at the door of a picture gal- ' lery with strict orders of the customary character. A sight- seer hastens along and is promptly halted. " Here, sir, you mug leave your cane at the door !" " But my friend, I haven't got any cane." "Then go back and get one. No one is allowed to pa's in here unless he leaves his cane at the door. Orders is orders."—San Francisco Bulletin. The latest story of police efficiency comes from New Jer- sey. A small boy happened to be crossing a canal bridge in Newark just as another small boy fell into the water. A policeman asked the boy on the bridge whether he could swim. The boy said he could, and with great presence of mind the policeman thereupon dropped him over the railing into the canal. After a hard struggle the boy who was dropped in succeeded in re3cuing the one who fell in. The policeman has not yet been promoted for his bravery. An Ohio correspondent becomes sponsor for the following, ; which, as a matter of fact, he wishes to put on record. Whittaker is one of the richest men in those parts and has made his money by driving sharp bargains. His hired man was one day going along a public road with a load of hay, when he overturned it upon a cow. The poor thing was smothered to death before they could get her out. Her owner, Jones, called upon Mr. Whittaker the next day, and demanded payment for the loss of his cow. "Certainly," said Mr. Whittaker, "what do you think she was worth ? " "Well, about ten dollars," said Jones. "And how much did you get for the hie and tallow?" "Ten dollars and a half." "Oh we'l, then you owe me just half a dollar." Jones was mystified, and Whittaker very fierce in his de- mand, and before Jones could get the thing straight in his mind, he forked over the money.—Harp's Monthly. A good story is told by Purser Neppens, of the Cunard tine :—" It is a rule, sir," said a ste‘vard to a tall, fair pas- senger, "to put on a-frock coat at dinner." This was after the vessel had been two days at sea. The passenger per- sisted in wearing his suit of light tweed, and the request was reiterated on the following day, which happened to be a stormy one. The vessel lurched heavily, but the passenger appeared in a frock coat of exquisite fineness. The contents of a plate of soup, however, soon destroyed its gloss, and the "gentleman retired abruptly in confusion. He said nothing, however, till Liverpool was reached, when, placing a letter in the hands of the purser, he desired him to give it to the manager of the line. Its contents were as follows :

The Line, To the Etrl of Addle. Dr. To spoiling one frock coat to oblige the Company. £7 73. N.8.-I.!ght tweed is more appropriate for grease spots than black cloth in heavy weather. E MITT 1.7 D War:cert.—A sister of John Hampden, who had married Robert Waller, of Agmondesham, in Backingham- shire, becae the mmother of Edmund Waller, the poet. Ed- mund Waller was born in 16)5, and inherited a large for- tune, by the death of hi 3 father, while he was stillyoung. His mother sent him to Eton and to Cambridge, and he was member for Agmonde3ham, when yet but a youth oi seven- teen, in the last Parliament of James I. En the earlier years of Charles 1., Edmund Waller, who, when in the cpuntry, was living at Beaconsfield, shone at Court, and married a lady of great fortune. She added to his wealth and died. Then as a widower of five-and-twenty he sang otothe beauty of the Lady D wothy Sidney, who aftervfffids was married to the Earl of Sunderland. She is celebrated as Waller's Sacharissa. Waller married a lady named Breese and had thirteen children. Both he and Lady Sun- derlani!, his Seeharissa, lived to ho very old, and were friends in old age. "When, Mr. Waller," said the old lady once," "will you write such fine verses to me again?" To which the poet replied, "Oh, madam, when your ladyship is as young again."—" Cassell's Library of Enqlish Litvature" for Augest. Tug StsKiN.—lt has often been matter for snrprise that this sweet docile, pretty, and amusing little bird is nOt bettor known, though certainly its merits are fast attractink atteu, tion ; and befbre long, if the supply of Goldfineheebecome3 exhausted, the S isk in may possibly supply its piece as a cage. bird. Better known in London, and in some other parts of England, as the Alierdevine, it may be that the double name has mystified arneteur ornithologists ; but from the members lately imported from Germany, it is seldom that a well con- stituted aviary is destitute of one of these sprightly little birds. Since no mention of the bird appears in the Rev. Gilbert White's" History of Selborne "—and he wee a most observant and true naturalist—it would appear almost as if these little winter visitants were unknown around that dis- trict. The plumage of the Siskin, together with its other natural advantages gives it a very high position in the list of Finches. Its beauty is indeed beyond gainsaying a brilliant lemon-yellow pervading its plumage throughout; and its celeur is thrown into especial contrast by the deep- ness of the black of the head and rest of the plumage. Several inetences hive been recorded of Siskins breeding in confinement ; and it may be that the patience and persever- aces of breedere may in the dim fu are make the Siskin a rival progenitor of the original Green Canary. The Siskin even at the present day mates freely with the Canary ; and the mules produced are handsome birds, and especially sweet songsters.—" Familiar Wild Birds" for August. THE GREAT ERUPTION OF VESUVIUS.—It happened for- tunately for modern times that the greet eruption of Mount Vesuvius wee described with considerable fulness by a very competent observer—Pliny the Younger. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, was residing in his villa ore the Misenian promon- tory when the awful catastrophe occurred. The promontory is situated about twenty miles from Vesuvius, and the sum- mit of the mountain is clearly seen across the Bay of *Naples. On the morning of the 24th of August, the elder Pliny perceived a cloud of unusual form and character rising from the distant cone, and spreading out laterally from a slender stem, like the figure of a pine tree. Such an appearance would have attracted the attention of any man, but especially of a man such as Pliny, whose love of know- ledge was an absorbing passion, and who is ehiefly known to modern times as the author of a Natural History full of learning, of varied observation, and of amazing credulity. Shortly afterwards, urgent appeals for assistance arrived from the dwellers about Vesuvius. Pliny was at that time commander of the fleet, and he directed that some of his largest vessels should be got ready, and steered to the chief points of danger, with a view to saving the people whose houses were situated on the lower slopes of the mountain. He himself set sail in a light Liburnian cutter, and pro- ceeded across the 'bay, which was now terribly agitated. The approach of night showed more clearly the appalling nature of the calamity; for what had been the darkness of smoke during the intense light of a Neapolitan noon be- came the glare of fire when darkness had descended from the zenith. The philosopher passed the night at the house of a friend living at Stabim, but towards morning was roused by his attendants, who reported that the court-yard was being rapidly filled with ashes. Frequent shocks of earthquake added to the horror of the moment, and the darkness produced by the unnatural smoke and vapour was so intense that it was necessary to kindle torches to light the fugitives on their way. Their design was to reach the shore, and embark on one of the ships; but the waves were so tumultuous that all the vessels had _departed. Pliny was corpulent, and afflicted With a difficulty of breathing; soon getting wearied, belay down on the ground, and refused to move any further. The greater number of his companions continued their flight. but two of the servants remained with their master until he was overpowered by the sulphurous blasts from the vol- came. Three days later his body was found by his nephew, without any marks of violence, and presenting the appear- ance rather of sleep than of death. Pliny the Younger was only eighteen at the time; but in two letters addressed to Tacitus.he.hes given the details of this great convulsion. The writer had refused to accompany his uncle across the ,bey, but observed the phenomenon from Misenum, and the particulars of his relative's death he collected from the re- ports of others. The effect of the eruption was extremely capricious; for, while Herculanenra and Pompeii were des- troyed, several places between them were almost untouched. This is attributable to the shifting of the wind, which ear- ned the fire and cinders sometlle3 in one direction, and sometimes in another, while passing round particular locali- ties. Of the two cities, Pompeii and Herculanenen, the former Antlered the least, if we can make any distinction where both were blotted out from existence. Whereas Pompeii was covered mainly with ashes to a depth not greater than fifteen feet, Herculaneum was engulfed with streams of lava, or liquid mud, to which later eruptions have added, until the total depth now varies from seventy to a hundred and twenty feet. In both eases the cities were so completely covered up that the knowledge of their sites was forgotten in a few generations, and it was not until the year 1706 that Herculaneum was discovered by the sinking of a well in the village of Resina, which revealed the pre- sence of ancient mosaics.—From "Cassell's Illustrated Universal History" for August. Mrs. TI —, one of a family a .------...._ number of whose members had died of consumption, was, after severe exposure to a snowstorm, seized with a serious conch and expectoration, accompanied with loss of flesh. Eximinetion by a physician showed that one lung was seriously affected. She was wholly confined to her room; ani everything that medical attendance and loving care cool I do to mitig ate her suffering was done, but ineffectually. The depressing night-sweats continued, together with loss of rest from repeated fits of coughing. Losing all faith in medicine, some six or eight months ago its use was wholly abandoned, and the use of nourishing diet only continued. About ten weeks ago the patient's attention was directed to a newspaper paragraph recommending hot water as a remedy for consumption. Feeling that little harm could en.ne from its use, she determined to test it. At the moment of retiring, a large tumbler of shot water, in which the juice of a lemon had been mixed to free it from nausea, was taken. In a few moments a glow of warmth would pervade the lungs, chest, itc., quickly followed by the most refreshing sleep, which would be unbroken by any cough, and the patient would awake in the morning rested and strengthened. A few days ago she was seized with a fit of coughing, daring which was coughed up into her mouth a small stone about the size of a pea—formed of sulphate of lime, I believe, and usually considered a symptom of the healing of a cavity in the lung. Whether this marked im- provement was due to the use of the hot water, I cannot venture to say; but its beneficial influence in securing sweet sleep and exemption from coughing at night was so marked that I should like some of your readers to test it with their consumptive friends, and give, through your Notes, the results of their experience.—Cl anthers' s Journal. EXCAVATIONS AT EPIIESUS.—Mr. A. J. B. Beresford Hope sends to The Times a brief statement from Mr. J. F. Wood, the able and persevering excavator of the ruins of the Temple of Diana and Ephesus, of his proceedings during the past season under many difficulties, and those heavy, which he was enabled to overcome through the cordial help accorded to him by her Majesty's Government, encouraged as he also was by the good will of the trustees of the British Museum. In March of the present year, the sanction of the trustees having been obtained, Mr. Wocd was authorised by the committee to proceed to Ephesus and resume the exca- vations which had been so long in abeyance for want of funds. The freehold of the site of the Temple had been purchased by the trustees of the British Museum during the time of the former excavations. Their right to resume the works seemed accordingly to be clear, although the question of the privilege of removing the sculptures which might he found was more disputed. Mr. Wood, however, had not ',long resumed his work when the Mudir of the district visited the spot and reported their recommencement to the Kaimac- han of Scala Nova, who in his turn reported the same to the Governor of Smyrna, and in due time the Mudir received his written instructions to stop the excavations. In obedi- ence then to the ittimation of the nadir, Mr. Wood sus- pended the work which he had then eXrried on for 14 days, and took the first boat for Constantinople to obtain a fresh permit from the Ottoman Government. This interruption delayed operations for several weeks, but happily the re- quired document was eventually obtained through the effectual good offices of Lord Granville and of the Embassy I at 'Constantinople, and in three days from the time when the request was submitted to the Sultan, the permit was handed to Mr. Wood by the Minister of Public Instruction. Mr. Wood then returned without delay and resumed the ex- cavations. By this time the cool weather had passed away and the hot season had set in, but as he was anxious to make some important discovery before abandoning the work till the autumn, Mr. Wood persevered until June 15, when he was forced to stop, for not only did the heat prevent the eworkmen from doing a fair day's work, but the water still stood in the excavations at a level which prevented the re- covery of the stones which could be felt through the mud. Several interesting inscriptions and fragments of sculpture were, however, secured. The latter evidently belonged to the pediment at the east end of the Temple. The most interesting of these was the leg of a male figure in high re- lief, somewhat larger than life. Mr. Hope writes:—"At a comthittee meeting held on July 24, it was decided to authorise Mr. Wood to return to Ephesus in September and I resume the excavations. The committee was justified in this decision by the fact that a large area had been opened up to an average depth of 17ft. in the few weeks of work during the spring and early summer, while the stones which could only be felt at that time through the mud and water could be easily removed in the autumn after the water will have subsided for a depth of several feet. I need hardly impress upon the archteological public that it is most de- sirable that they should subscribe liberally, if they desire the success of this most interesting exploration. If it is carried on as it onghtto be to the extent proposed—namely, to the Temple, m pl e .o tnht ee rr efsauel et wofillthperobcoalbolnynbaedethwehuicnheasruthrrinogunbdoedththoef beautiful sculptures and inscriptions possessing historical value. The discoveries which reach England will be placed in the gallery which is to be devoted at the British Museum to the Ephesian antiquities, and will be a great addition of permanent value to the national art treasures."

CELERY.—Late plantings of this will require watering when the weather is dry for three or four days, and if it has grown sufficiently an inch of soil may be put to it after a good watering. Tile contents of the washing tubs should be applied to it. Tanking cannot be of much service until 3in. or 4in. of growth has been made. The manure in the trench ought to support it with plenty of clear water up to that stage. Crops that are further advanced should have a liberal application of manure water. The urine of all animals has a beneficial effect upon it, if not given too strong at first. So has liquid made from fresh fcecal mat- ter, soaked in water, adding a handful of salt to eight gal- lons of the liquid, allowing it ample time to dissolve. This, after being further diluted, will have the same proportion of saline matter as urine. ONIONS should be sown now, taking advantage of a dry day to tread the ground, and raking it so as to get an even surface. Stretch the line and make drills half an inch deep and Bin, apart, and after every fifth row allow one foot, so as to permit them being weeded without treading over the ground sown. There are many varieties which find place in seedsmen's catalogues. We have found the foliowing very good :—Red and White Tripoli, Giant Rocco, and White Lisbon. SHALLOTS are showing symptoms of approaching matu- rity, and a few sunny days will finish them sufficiently to. be taken up and stored in an open, airy situation for a few days, till the whole of the moieture by which they are sur- rounded has entirely disappeared, when they may be cleaned stored in a smaller compass. 'THOST GARDEN.—Carnations: The soil which we ad- vised to be placed round these in readiness for layering should now be made use of. For this operation we select a dry period to do those that necessitate treading the border to get at them. Thoie that are easily reached from the path'mav be done any time. The young shoots of these and Pinks are frequently termed "grass." We will, there- fore, say if the grass is healthy and strong that five layers will be sufficient from each stool or parent plant, and the surplus must be removed. The others must be taken one by one, and have the bottom leaves trimmed off to about the third node from the base. There should be a sufficient num- ber ef pegs in readiness, and it will facilitate matters if they are first taken and a sufficient number distributed to each stool, so that nothing remains but for the operator to take each grass and make an incision upwards one inch long and half through the stem. If the head of the grass is now placed tolerably upright it will tend to open the incision; press the cut towards the soil, guiding the tongued portion into the soil without damaging it, for it is from this portion roots are to emanate. The pegs, which should be about 4in. or sin. long, should then be thrust into the soil until the hooked portion comes right on the grass, when soil and peg may be further pressed by the combined action of both hands. The pegs may be made of wire, pieces from the boughs of trees, or pieces of willows doubled. After the whole are completed they should receive a sprinkling of water from a can with a moderately fine distributor. Heavy waterings will only wash the soil from the layers, and all that is required now is to settle the soil. The Windflower or Anemone should be sown now in light, rich soil having a south aspect. It is best to sow in drills 6in. distant for convenience of cleaning. The seeds being surrounded with so much woolly matter is difficult to separate, so we mix it with some moderately moist sand, which enables us to distribute it more evenly. THE WlNDOW.—Geraniums of the pelargonium section should be turned on their sides if they are outside. The open air is the best place for them, and far superior to any glass structure. Therefore lay them down with the pots to the sun—the latter will be able to act on wood acncl foliage. Laying them secures them from being watered by heavy showers when they do not require it. We haxe not yet seen a cottager treat this plant properly. So that whatever success they may have is purely accidental. At this time of the year the plant requires reet, but the cottager never thinks of giving it one. To bring about this rest, in addi- tion to sun and air, water must be gradually withheld; but ' before attempting this, it must be observed that the current year's growth must show symptoms of turning brown two or three inches long. The cottager should ahn at resting the plants without shrivelling them. Whilst on their sides they will be sure to require turning up to be watered a few times, and after the water has passed through replace them as before, excepting that the side next to the ground should be uppermost. This will allow the same advantages to the whole of the plant, so that its wood will be brown for seve- ral inches in length, and quite hard where it comes to be , cut or pruned. Having in view the forthcoming flower , show to be held at Preston. we advise Fuschias to be sup- plied with manure water three times a week. That made from pure guano is good, and no more should be used than will colour the water, or the probabilities are that every bud will fall off. Clay's fertiliser is Neatly good and very cheap, as well as being easily procured in small quantities, which is not the case with guano. No flowers should be .Ilowed to expand until ten days before the show. Gera- niums should be similarly fed with the liquid manure. The dower Weds may now be left on, but any already on the point of expanding will be useless in a month's time. Bal- sams must have all the buds picked off in which the colour iis visible, for they expand rapidly, and the plants are only tt their best for a fortnight, and they can be had in perfec- 1 non at any stated day by exercising a little judgment and i skill in these matters.

SOME NOTES ON VICTORIA. No. I. Thanks mainly to its gold deposits and the vigour with which it has carried on and is still spiritedly pursuing its mining operations, Victoria is the most advanced of the Australasian colo- nies. And Melbourne, the capital of Victoria, is well entitled to the distinction of being styled" The Queen City of the South." The New South Welsh people hold that Sydney, the older capital, ought to be awarded the palm, and there is no doubt that Sydney, with its magnifi- cent harbour, is a most beautiful spot. On the other hand the South Australians are demonstrative in their praises of Adelaide, which they declare is a more charming city than either Sydney or Melbourne. It is, however, en- deniable that in extent, in the splendour of its public and other buildings, and in its enterprise, Melbourne is far away ahead of any of the Australasian capitals. In the colony of Victoria there are about 900,000 people, and it is a remark- able fact that one-third of these live in Melbourne and its suburbs. "A bad look out for Victoria," some will say, "that so large a proportion of her population is centred in the metropolis." Just so ; but it has to be added that in pro- portion to her area, Victoria is much more equally settled than the rest of the colonies ; that manufactures have aggre- gated a great number of people in Melbourne, and that these 300,000 people in Melbourne and its suburbs have as much space to dwell on as the whole of the district included in the jurisdiction of the Metropolitan Board of Works of London. So that though building operations have for a long time been and still are exceedingly active, the city has no appearance of being crowded. The vital statistics which are important on the point show, indeed, that the city is a remarkably healthy one notwithstanding the absence of a good system of drainage. Viewed from the dome of the Exhibition Building or from any similar elevation, Mel- bourne is in truth a very fair city to look upon, and the colony has every warrant for claiming it as a wonderful place, especially seeing that it is only about 40 years of age! Melbourne was laid out by Mr. Hoddle, the first Sur- veyor- General, on the parallel lines of Philadelphia. Bourke- street, named in honour of a Colonial Governor; Collins-at., called after the name of the official who rendered such signal service to the future settlement by reporting against the suitability of the locality as a convict settlement; and Flin- ders-street in commemoration of the explorer, are the three leading thoroughfares in Melbourne. They run from eat to west, an:l by them trend in the same direction narrower streets, distinguished as Little Bourke, Collins, and Flinders- streets respectively. Collins-street is the Regent-iereet of Melbourne, and the " crack " thoroughfare of Australia. At the western end are the principal banks and insurance com- panies—institutions, both of them, which in these colonies are exceptionally successful. The best buildings in every small township are generally the branch banks, and the banks in Collins-street, Melbourne, are among the finest buildings of the kind anywhere. The eastern extremity of this street is mainly given up to the medical faculty, whose residences vie in proportions and taste with those of their wealthy clients, who may live in the a- istocratic suburbs of St. Kilda or Toorak. But the glory of Collins-street is in its "block." Collins-street " block " is an institution in which the ladies are more par- ticularly interested. It is a term applied to the central part of the street, where the " best" shops are, and where every week-day afternoon there promenade as gay a show of brightly-dressed women as can be found in any other part of the world. Victorian ladies devote a great amount of time and money to the questioa of what to wear, and feminine cos- tume in Melbourne is of the most pronounced type. The climate has, of course, much to do with this. You may see In Collins-street a display of fashion in ladies' habiliments quite eclipsirtg anything to be seen out of doors in the old country. Ladies go about here attired in rich and airy fabrics which, in England, are usually only to be seen at balls and parties, and a shabbily- dressed or plainly-dressed woman or girl you seldom see. The Collins-street " block " affords indirect testimony as to the wealth and prosperity of the colony. Another fact which adds to the importance of this thoroughfare is that in it, too, is the Exchange, formerly known as the Verandah." From hence there is telephonic communication to nearly every house of business and every public institution in the city, and the members by means of telegrams and news- papers from all parts are enabled to place themselves en rapport with what is occurring in the markets and com- mercial centres of the civilised world. No one visiting this Exchange at the busiest time of the day would deny that it furnishes a remarkable example of business activity. In Collins-street, too, are the principal club houses and the offices of the leading stock and station agents. Tnese " squatters' " agents play an important part in colonial life, and many of them have made lerge fortunes. It may interest my readers if I mention that at the present time two of Charles Dicken's sons carry on business as stock and sta- tion agents here under the sty le of Edward Bulwer Lytton Dickens and Company. But the main artery, the people's street of Melbourne, is Bourke-street, or rather Bourke-street East, with its theatres and other places of entertainment, its arcades, and its splendid market hall—" Paddy's market" it is called. Bourke-street at night, extensively illuminated with the electric light, presents an exceedingly animated appearance. and if it were on a dead level would be very suggestive of the London Strand. Saturday night's crush in Bourke-street is one of the sights of Melbourne, and it is the young Victorian's ambition to be in it. In Bourke-street West are several huge warehouses for the storage of two of Australia' mein products—wool and grain. These estab- lishments include the massive block 9 h.-..19n.,;ing to the premier Australian firm of R. Goldsborough and Company, Limited. Mr. Richard Gohisborough, the founder of the concern, came originally from Bradford, in Yorkshire, I believe, and the warehouses of the company are among the most colossal. And, speaking of warehouses, I may remark that those of the dry goods' and other importers in Flinders- street and Little Flinders-street, which are near the Mel- bourne Wharves, are quite as well built and as capacious as those in which Manchester or Bradford, the emporiums of the cotton and worsted trades in England, take pride. The ecclesiastical architecture of Melbourne is by com- parison a little behind hand, notwithstanding the fact that in the earlier days of the colony, all the sects, save the In- dependents, who would not participate, received liberal State assistance in the shape of land grants. It is understood that the dominant churches Anglican, Presbyterian, Catholic, and Wesleyan—each took slices in this way, which bring them in good sources of revenue ; but, however, that may be, the places of worship are not, I am bound to say, very imposing edifices. There are exceptions in Mel- bourne, as, for instance. the Saota Church, the Congrega- tional Church in Collins-street, the principal Weeleyan church, and St. Patrick's Roman Catholic Cathedral, the full design of which is not vet completed. Several ot the Anglican churches are decidedly mean, but under the reign df Bishop Moorhouse a better taste seems to be springing up in this direction, and a lead is being taken by the erection of a broad new Cathedral Church for the diocese of Mel- bourne. It is intended that this shall be a magnificent structure. Several years will have passed by ere the building is finished. I cannot pretend to allude to all the other public buildings with which Mel- bourne is exceptionally well supplied, but a few must be noted. The Town Hall in Swanoton-street, and the Public Library and Museum in the same thorough- fare, are both commanding structures. The former pos- sesses in its principal apartment the finest organ in the Southern Hemisphere, and on it are given periodical recitals after the manner of those common to some of the larger towns of the North of Eneland. The Public Library. Fine Art Gallery, and Technological Museum, all under one roof, are three highly creditable institutions. First place must be given to the Library, which in extent and convenience of classification occupies a very high position. There are close upon 150,000 volumes to refer to, and no ticket or pre- liminary of any sort is required in order to obtain a work to read. You consult the catalogues, go to the bay where the work is, take it out of the shelves, and sit down and peruse it. The Free Libraries which are established in most of the towns in the colony are conducted on much the same lines; and are purely for reference. Thus they are so much be- hind public free libraries in the old country. The Picture and Sculpture galleries which form the Fine Art department of this national repository are very popular. The pictures are of a high class, but fewer in number than one would wish. The sculptures are a stronger representa- tion. For the encouragement of art students facilities are ' given, as at South Kensington, for the copying of both sculptures and paintings, and the privilege appeers to be greatly prized, judging by the number of young persons who are daily engaged in the occupation. The gentlemen who have the control of this part of the building and the Technological Museum are empowered to render what assist- ance they can by loans, (Sze., to lc-al schools of design in the colony—institutions analogous to the schools of art in Eng- land; but, I think, in a more prosperous condition rela- tively. On the whole this Melbourne Pablio Library and Art Gallery is doing a grand work for the capital and for the colony. The showiest building, externally, in Melbourne is the Exhibition Building in Carlton Gardens. In this edi- fice, and in temporary annexes which are neer removed, was held the International Exhibition of 1880, an undertaking which gave a great stknulus to colonial industry, and at the same time informed foreigners of the vast resources of the country. There is a project talked of for utilising this pile as an industrial museum, but nothing is being done in the matter definitely ; and meanwhile the main hall is put to such occasional uses as bicycle tournaments, fancy fairs, and musical festivals. One of the wings is used as the Government Printing Office. In these colonies each Govern- ment does its own printing, the department of the Govern- ment printer being one of the branches of the Civil Service. On one of the hills on which the city proper is built—the Eastern Hill—stand Parliament House and the ;7Government Offices. The latter are composed,of two or three imposing blocks,'which would not de discredit to a great European Power. The fagade of the former is unbuilt—there being a difficulty about the stone to be employed—but the apart- ments which are finished, the two legislative chambers, the central hall, the library, &c, convey the impression that Victoria is determined to be to the front in its Parliamentary buildings. The Governor of the Colony, who receives £lO,OOO a year—more than is paid to any other of the Ass- rralian governors—is magnificently housed with a one- hundred-roomed residence, overlooking the banks of the Yarns. I ought to mention, perhaps, in this connection that the present occupier of Government House, the Marquis of Normanby, is fairly popular throughout Victoria. As , might be expected from a Yorkshire nobleman, he is a wil- ling patron of agriculture and out-door sports, and sport- loving Victoria. which is alsoaentliusiss'ically loyal theugh intensely democratic, likes to have the approval of vice- , egil sanction. Thus all the thoronglifares are which have their free libraries and newsrooms, their weekly wonderfully wide, and public parks, gardens, or recreation or bi-weekly journals, handsome public offices, and corn- grounds are numerous. This is 'most emphatically the case modious and well-furnished hotels. The dust of Melbourne is indeed a thing to be re- the lately defined counties they have practically yet to be membered, and it is likely to remain the curse of the place peopled. Four counties, for instance Weeah, Karkarooc, a long time to come, and until the "city fathers" carry out Millewa, and Croajingolong, had at the last census only a the contemplated plan of introducing wooden pavements in total population of 800. the busiest parts, and until the tree-planting, to which con- siderable attention has been paid, shall have developed its advantages. While speaking of the streets, I may mention another drawback which they very forcibly demonstrate. There is no efficient sewerage system. The drainage is surface, and is conducted by means of " gutters " into the river Yarra, which stream, as it Tuns through Melbourne to the out-fall into Hobson's Bay, is quite equal in filthiness to certain of those which pursue their slimy course through some of the North of England manufacturing towns, defiant of the existence of the Rivers Pollution Act. On a summer day in Melbourne, with the thermometer in the shade standing at 95 or 100, the aroma from these Melbourne gutters is not of the pleasantest character. The climatic conditions of life otherwise must of necessity be highly favourable, or the- objectionable arrangement adverted to would of itself render the city dangerous to the health of the inhabitants. Newcomers from the home country find the greatest amusement and novelty from a mode of conveyance which they see as soon as they get into Melbourne is the most popular street vehicle, and, along with the railways and the 'buses, a common medium of communication between the city proper and the suburbs. I speak of the covered wag- gonettes, which are styled cabs. They are a sort of cross between an Irish jaunting car and an express waggon. In addition to plying for private hire as at home, and as do the hansoms there are here, these " cabs " are found in great numbers on the 'bus routes, and they take you up for the ' same fare, which in most instances is threepence, a charge which, as money% goes in Victoria, must be deemed to be a low one. More may be said in another letter about the rail- way system of the colony, which is entirely in Government hands; but I may remark here that the Melbourne sub- urban railways are in their extent and in their convenience a great boon to the public, spite of many well-grounded complaints of managerial defects and administrative details. Were it not for the jolting which the 'buses, like the wag- gonettes, undergo in crossing the "gutters," I would pro- nounce them to be an exceedingly satisfactory mode of transit. The 'Bus Company, anticipating opposition from trams has determined to get tram powers for itself, and has applied to the Legislature for the requisite authority. Before long, therefore, tramways will be laid down, as they have been for some time in Sydney and Adelaide. The extensive use by the commercial and professional classes of the tele: phone has already been commented on. The more recent advance in electrical science, the electric light, is being taken advantage of quickly, and it is anticipated that ere another twelve months have elapsed the rich monopoly which has , the right to supply Melbourne and suburbs with gas (price ' 6s. 6d. per thousand) will find its income considerably diminished through the adoption in public buildings of the I electric illumination. Already the new light is utilised for the two Legislative Chambers, for one or two of the theatres, for the principal railway stations, and in other places. Having mentioned, the subject of lighting, the water supply may be next noted. Throughout the whole colony the question of water conservation is now receiving intelligent attention, and the water famines which in the drier regions have in past years caused great suffering and loss will now probably be rare. Melbourne itself has for a lengthened period been able to rejoice in an abundant pro- vision in this respect. The supply comes from the Yan Yean reservoir, which is situated about 20 miles out of the city in the Plenty ranges. A discolouration, accompanied by a smell which is irreverently designated the " Yan Yean stink," are frequently observable with the water, and it is not considered wise to use the liquid for drinking purposes until there has been a further filtration; but, on the whole, the supply must be regarded as a wonderfully good one. At the time of its completion the reservoir was said to be the largest artificial one in the world. It occupies an area of 1,300 acres. ' It is time I said something in this sketch of Melbourne of its public parks and gardens. The Botanical Gardens, the Fitzroy Gardens (which contain extensive avenues of Eng- lish trees), the Canton Gardens (with the Exhibition Build- ing in the centre), and the Zoological Gardens may be mentioned, among a number of others. The three first named are only a few minutes walk removed from the heart of the city. In the Botanical Gardens are to be found speci- mens of every kind known to naturalists, which, while arranged with an eye to scenic effect, are exceedingly valu- able from an educational Doha of view. Additions are con- stantly being made, and immense care is taken by the curator to maintain for the place both a scientific and a picturesque fame. Withal I think the umbrageous shades of Fitzroy Gardens are more in request, and on a sweltering day there is nothing more grateful to the sense than to find refuge in one of the cool glades of this favourite resort. On the week days a small fee is exacted for admission to the Zoological Gardens, which form an enclosure within a breezy domain known as Royal Park. On the Sunday the , "Zoo" is open to the public free, and the boon is taken ad- vantage of very largely. The collection of birds, animals, and reptiles, already a very good one, is continually being , improved bygifts to the society in charge of the gardens, and by judicious purchases made by the Director, who is to be congratulated on the good sense and taste he displays in the arrangement and housing of the various spechnens. The old country has to thank these colonies for several " sugges- tions"—a fact which Australians are not a little proud of— and I fancy the zoological authorities at Regent's Park could pick up a few "wrinkles" from the Melbourne Zoo- logical Gardens which would be of some use to them in their older and much more extensive establishment. A word or two respecting the suburbs of Melbourne, which cover a large tract of land. They are, as a rule, laid out very attractively, and are all easily accessible from the city, so that there prevails in Melbourne the desire to live away from the business centre, which is characteristic of the big cities in the old country. Each Melbourne suburb seems to have pretensions which stand in the way of a com- prehensive scheme of local government for the capital and its environs, hence there are no end of separately consti- tuted authorities. While Melbourne proper has its City Council, the suburbs of Fitzroy, Hotham Collingwood, St. Kilda, Prahran, Richwood, Emerald Hill, and others have each their municipal boards and staffs, accommodated for the most part in handsome town halls and offices. Every municipality in Victoria which has an income of £20,000 annually is entitled to be proclaimed a city, therefore some of these suburbs are "cities," as Fitzroy, Richwood, and Collingwood. This divided authority, however flattering to the vanity of the people in office, cannot be regarded as the best arrangement, and it is not surprising that among the subjects urged on the attention of the Colonial Legislature is that of forming a Board of Works for jurisdiction over the whole metropolitan area. Though about one-third of the population of Victoria [which, as a colony, has an area as large as England and Scotland] is to be found in the bounds of Melbourne and suburbs, the colony presents more of the aspects of general settlement than any other of the Australian group, and "up country" towns are numerous and some of them well worth a visit. These centres give more of a home character to Victoria than a stranger who has only heard of vast tracts occupied as sheep walks and cattle runs would be led to ex- pect. Every year, with increasing land selections and the growing tendency there is to sub-divide large holdings, agri- culture is getting more and more associated with pasturing, and what with farming, viniculture, hop and other kinds of cultivation, the face of the country is rapidly changing. There are little towns like Sale, in Gippoland Penalla in the north-eastern district, Hamilton in the west, and Horsham in the Wintmera country, which are remarkably flourishing agricultural centres, comparing very favourably with third class English towns in everything but their extent of popu- lation; and the number of these places all, or nearly all, in direct railway communication with Melbourne is astonish- ing when thought of in connection with the fact that the colony only a few years ago turned its attention to farming as a profitable pursuit. The gold-mining towns are, how- ever, still to the fore in spirit and activity. Of these may be mentioned Stawell, Clunes Creswick, Daylesford, and the cities of Ballarat and Sandhurst. Between Ballarat and Sandhurst there exists some such rivalry as that which pervades Manchester and Liverpool or Leeds and Bradford. It is hard to decide the claims of each for pre-eminence. Ballarat, while the elder, is also the prettier of the two places. It has great natural advantages: the hills forming its site setting off to the full the many

Commission. Papers received by the Australa mail state that Mr. J: E. Redmond, M.P., and his brother, Mr. W. Redmond, tiaVe delivered a series of lectures in Melbourne in aid of the Irish National Land Leagu,, and that their visit is un- favourab!y viewed in the colony, Upwards Of 30,000 persons assembled in Trafalgar-square, London, on Monday, to protest against the eoutiuued elusion of Mr. Bradlaugh from his sea', and a resolution was passed calling for the dissolution of the House which persisted in so unlawful a course of action. The ifentorzal Diplontatique contains an announcement to the effect that Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., proposes to go to France very shortly in order to confer with M. de Lesseps on the best means of establishing a definitive understanding between Her Majesty's Government and M. do Lesseps. Sir Richard Cross and other members of the Irish Prisons Committee, which has nor commenced its labours, will spend a considerable portion of the recess in Ireland, anl will then pay a personal visit of inspection to the prisons which are especially the subject of inquiry, and in which the accommodation is stated to be either unsuitable or in- adequate. Sir John Lubbock, Mr. Erringtan, Mr. Salt, Viscount Lymington, Mr. Raikes, Sir L. Playfair, Viscount Euilyn, Mr. Childers, Mr. Dawson, Mr. S. Morley, Mr. J. Campbell, Herbert, Mr. J. N. Richardson, Mr. EL Gladstone, and Mr. Pell have been nominated as the Select Committee on he Administration of the Votes for Education, Science, and

Art. Determined resistance will (sain the Daily News) be offered on the Conservative side to any attempt to pass this session the Court of Criminal Appeal Bill, which, after pro- longed fighting, has been reported by the Grand Committee to the house. Sir R. Cross will move the discharge of the order for consideration of the bill, on the ground that it is impossible at this period of the session to discuss it. A Blue Book, issued on Tuesday night, contains further correspondence regarding the affairs of the Gold Coast. The despatches included data from March, 1882, to July eith last, and relate to various subjocts, such as the rising against the King of Ashanti, alleged atrocities by the Monarch, and reports on the gold mining districts. The papers are ac- companied by a number of maps and plans. A Blue Book was issued on. Monday, containing further cotrespondence respecting the affairs of Zululand. It ex- tends from 'April 19 to July 12, 1883, and is principally composed of despatches from Sir Henry Bulwer, Her Majesty's Special Commissioner in Natal, to Lord Derby, complaining of the aggressive action of Cetewavo since his restoration. Lord Derby, in reply, recpasted Sir Henry to warn Cetewayo, in the strongest and most sofernc manner, against infringing the independence of the reserve, or dis- turbing the Zulus residing there.

PERSONAL. The Duke of Edinburgh attained his nth birthday on Monday. Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone visited her Majesty at Osborne on Saturday. The Earl and Countess of Derby hive left their residence in St. James's-square, London, for Keaton. The Duchess of Tack presided on Saturday at the cere- mony of opening the west wing of the West London Hos-

pital. Mr. John -Holmee, M.P., will proceed to America to represent the Board of Trade at the, opening of the Pacific Railway. The Princess Louise has promised to send a number of her paintings, both in tAI and watercolour, to the Boston Exhibition. Intimation has been received at Balmoral that the Queen, accompanied by the Princess Beatrice, will arrive on or about the 24th of August. Baronetcies have been granted to Dr. Andrew Clarke and Mr. Prescott Hewett, Sergeant-Surgeon Extraordinary to her Majesty. The Earl of Lathom and Lord Elphinstone have gone on a tour in the United States and Canada, and contemplate an absence from home of abcrurthree or four months. His Grace the Duke of Westminster has given a thousand pounds and a site of six acres of land towards the erection of a church at Caerfalhoch, Northop, near Chester. The Rev. Alfred Barry, D.D.. Principal of King's College and Canon of Westminster, has accepted the post of Bishop of Sydney, Metropolitan of New South Wales and Primate of Aus'ralia. Mr. Thomas Burt,.M.P., sails to-day {Saturday) for the United States per Cunard steamer Scythia. He will visit the mining districts in Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Illinois, and will be absent, from England about.two months. The Dundee Town Council on Tuesday last, unanimously resolved to confer the freedom of the burgh on E ids Rose- berry, Campardown, and Dalhousie, on the occasion of the opening of Dundee University College in October next. Admiral Lord Alcester presented the prizes, on Monday, at Bayley Flower Show, form-led by the Marquis of Hert- ford in connection with the Labourers' Improvement Society. The Maiquis of Hertford was present, and Lord Alcester was received very enthusiastically. The approaching visit of Lord Coleridge to the United State.s will be officially recognised by the Government of Washington. The American Attorney General has placed himself in communication with the Lord Chief Justice, and will represent the American Government at the reception.. Mrs. Langtry has, it is stated, cleared in her American season over £25,000. After making a short provincial tour she will return to America abut the .16th of October, and open an engagement in Montreal on the 29th of October. After her American trip she will go to Australia for ten weeks... On Wednesday, the marriage between Miss Mildred Mary Josephine de Trafford, eldest daughter of Sir Humphrey axle'', Lady Annette de Trafford, of Trafford Park, and the Hon. Captain Charles Bertram Bellew, eldest.son and heir of Lord Bellew, of Barmeash, Dunleer, county Louth, Ireland, was was celebrated at All Saints, Barton-upon-Irwell. Mr. Tleomes Heaton, chief steward of the Sarmatian, of the Allan Line, has just received a handsome present from her Royal Highness the Princess Louise in the form of a geld pencil case, bearing an appropriate inscription, accom- panied with a letter expressive of her Royal Highness's appreciation of Mr. Heaton's uniform coartesy towards her- self and suite whilst passengers to Canada.

River, Tilt far from Ponta Negro, by which two officers of net Majesty's ganbAt Stork and a civilian lost their lives. ['he Stork, wh;cli is commanded by LieutenAnt and C on- ma.lder Arthur illennerhasset, and which arrived on the Wes Coast of Africa a few months since, had been otdered sou;tl to St. Paul de LoandA, and on her way thither she called in at the place mentioned. The office's met with a cordial reception from Mr. Prenslan, .factory agent, under whose auspices a sporting trip in the Mayumba seems to have been arranged. Mr. Prenslau, Lieutenant Blenner- basset, Lieutenant Henry Leeke, and Mr. Robert Anderson, surgeon of the Stork, were together in a boat, when they were attacked by a hippopotamus. The animal, probabl wounded, and thus infuriated, made a ferocious and deter- mined onslaught on the boat, and all the efforts of the occu- pants to beat it off were unavailing. The struggle was a fierce one, and in the end the boat was swamped and cap— sized, and all the occupants were thrown struggling into the water. With great difficulty Lieutenant Blennerhasset was saved, but Lieutenant Leeke, Dr. Anderson, and Mr. Yrenslau were drowned. Lieutenant Leeke, who had been appointed to the Stork for navigating duties in lien of a sub-lieutenant, attained his present rank in August 1881, and served on board the Achilles during the E4yptian war. Dr. Anderson enteced the navy only in August, 1881, and this was his first service on a foreign station.

ANTI-JEWIeII Rtor IN RUSSIA. Accordine te an official communication, a mob at Ekateri- noslav made an attack upon the Jews in the town on the 2ed instant, which is &lid to have been provoked by an in- sult offered by a Jew to a peasant woman. The military had to be called out to restore order, and attacked the rioters, who are mestly road labourers, killing ten and wounding thirteen of their number. A telegram received from Ekateri- neslav states that the Town Council have resolved to devote 5,000 roubles as compensation to the Jews for loeses sustained by them. The council atso decided to give shelter in the public buildings of the town to those Jews who had been rendered homeless. FiGraTINCT IN TONQUIN. 700 KILLED AND WOUNDED. An official despatch from Saigon, dated Sunday evening, announces the receipt of intelligence from Tonquin confirmino. the news of the successful sortie made by Colonel Brdens from Namdinh on the 19th ult. The enemy, whose forces were entirely composed of Annamites, lost 700 in killed and wounded. The French captured seven guns, besides a large quantity of small arms. The positions taken were, however, reoccupied by the Annamites immediately after the departure of the French troops. The Annamite general in commend is stated to be among the killed. The loss on the French side was teelve killed and wounded. Mt Charles iron, the French Minister of Marine, has re- signed, and it is believed that he will be succeeded by Ad- miral Peyron. M. Hartmann, the Russian Nihilist, has arrived in Lon- don, accompanied by M. Dubois, a French Communist, They are arranging for a Socialist congress. It is reported that an accord has been arrived at between the Vaticen and the French Government on the chief questions relating to the ecclesiastical policy of the , republic. MEETING OF Emvernerrs.—According to arrangement, the Emperor of Germany and the Emperor of Austria met at Ischl on Wednesday. The interview is described as having been most cordial. Two dwarfs have been married in Urbana, Ohio. Charles Wooley, the groom, is 4ft, Sin, in height and weights 1181 be. The bride, Miss Florence Bitman, is 4ft. high and weighs 1081bs. Both are over 21 years of age. ITALY AND MOROCCO.—A powerful Italian fleet has been stationed on the coast of Morocco, and it is in a semi-official manner declared that it will not be withdrawn before a num- ber of claims of Italy on that State are complied with. THE RUSSIAN " ENVOY " IN AFGRANISTAN.—News has , arrived at Lahore from a trustworthy source to the effect that the Russian merchant who is called by the Afghans a Russian envoy has arrived at the lemeer's Camp at Gun- damuk, and had an interview with the Ameer. ELECTION RIOT IN THE UNITED STATES.—Daring an election riot at Bryantsville, in the United States, arising out a 'dispute concerning the vote of d white man, who had sold himself to both tides, two negroes were killed and two mortally wounded, while three other persons, two being white men, were seriously injured. The celebration of the Luther jubilee in November will generally take the form of special religious ceremonies at all the places intimately connected with the person of the Reformer, such as Wittenberg, Eisenach, Erfart, Eisleben, Worms, &c., and free public lectures will be delivered by pious and learned men all over the country. A despatch from Ottawa states that owing te the threats of the Irish Invineibles a guard will be mounted at Rideau Hall, after the arrival of Lord Lansdowne, and will be sup- plied with ball cartridge. It is uncrerstoed that the Marquis of Lorne and Princess Louise will remain at Quebec until the arrival of the new Governor-General. DEA."'2H OF THE FATTEST WOMAN IN THE WORLD.— American papers report the death of "the fattest woman in the world," Fanna Conley, a member of one of the special curiosities of Nathan's Cleveland Circus. She was found dead, lying on her face, in the sleeping waggon of the com- pany, and the presumption was that she was unable to turn in her bed without assistance, and was 90 suffocated. She venighed 4971 b. CHOLERA IN EGYPT.—The cholera mortality in Egypt is gradually decreasing, and the official report received at the War Office on Thursday was again satisfactory. Daring the preceding 24 hours thee bad been only two cases of , cholera amongst the British troops—one at Suez and the other at Rimleh—and no death had been reported. The Nile at Khartoum is now stationary, and the appre- hended over flow of the river in Upper Egypt has not occurred. CETEWAYO REPORTED TO HE ALlVE.—Several messen- gers lately asked Mr. Robertson, a missionary in -Central Zululand, what he would do or say if Cetewayo were to come back, thus giving rise to the suspicion that the King is not dead. Zitrebu is resting quiet. The Governor in Council has decided that Lagalibilele, by an act of grace, may return under restrictions forbidding the exercise of tribal authority, and subjeeting him to the chief Teleleku. Strenuous opposition is anticipated from the Legislature. A REFORMING PRINCE.—A statement is published that the Prince of Montenegro, who some time ago closed all the cafes and drinking shops in his dominion, regarding them as schools of effeminacy, extravagance, and corruption, and abolished all titles, sothat while formerly every Other man in Montenegro was an " Excellency," now even the ministers have to be content with plain" Mr.," has recently issued an interdict against all "luxurious wearing apparel," including cravats, gloves, walking-sticks, parasols, and umbrellas. MILITARY REVOLT I 5 SPAIN.- -The intelligence of the revolutionary outbreak early on Sunday morning among the Spanish troops at Badajoz,.at first kept secret by the Au- therities, is now fatly confirmed. The garrison made a pro- nunciamento in favour of the establishment of a republic, based on the constitution of 1869, under the presidency of Senor Ruiz Z arilla. The troops at Badajoz have fraternised with the people. Their number is between SRO and 700 men Several infantry regiments were deepatched to put down the movement, which is now regarded as at an end. ANOTHER AT rE:KFT TO SWIM NIAGARA. He intends to have a dummy figure made about his own weight aad size, and to east it into the Rapids before making the attempt. By this means he hopes to ascertain the steength and ten- in England,

TIIE STATE OF IRELAND. THE IRISH INFORMERS IN AUSTRALIA. The informers, Michael Kavanagh and Joseph Hanlon, have written a letter declaring that they were shipped to Australia by the detective police. They had anDlied to to! sent to the colonies on account of the strong 'feeling pre- vailing in Ireland against them. It is understood to be in- tended to reship the informers back to England.

Her Majesty's ironclad Nelson has arrived at Sydney with the Irish informers on board. At Dublin, on Wednesday, Joseph Poole was committed for trial, charged with the murder of John Kenny, in Seville-place. The Lord-Lieutenant and the Countess Spencer arrived from England in Dublin, on Tuesday, and took up their re- sidence at the Viceregal Lodge. 'Hie anniversary of the death of the late Charles James Kickham, one of the 1965 Fenian convicts, is to be celebrated at Mullinabone on Sunday, the 26:h instant. In charging the City of Duelin grand jury, on Tuesday. Mr. Justice Johnston said the CASOS are not above the average, and the number and average would favourably com- pare with other large cities. At the Sligo Assizes, Edward Fox, Patrick Connelly, and William Dreskin, were found guilty of the manslaughter of Thomas Gibbons, son of Lord Ardilaun's herd, and were each sentenced to 20 years' penal servitude. Preliminary arrangements are in progress with a view to the formation of more than half a dozen limited liability companies for the development of the fisheries and fish trade in Ireland, consequent upon the recent passing of Mr. Blake's Bill. Mr. Michael Devitt, on Thursday, on visiting Hollyhill, near Loughrea, found the dead body of a man named Burke in a ditch. Mr. Davitt charged the Loughrea relieving- officer with negligence, and wired the particulars to Mr. Healy, M.P. On Tuesday, the collector-general of rates for Dublin was appointed creditors' assignee, as being the petitioning credi- tor in the bankruptcy of the mterdered informer, James Carev, who was adjedicated for arrears of rates exceeding £l2O on house property in the city. In response to urgent invitations to visit the United , States during the Parliamentary recess. Mr. Parnell has telegraphed to the Executive Committee of the Irish National League in America that he will be unable to visit the United States until after the general election. Father Walsh, who was the treasurer of the Irish League in America, has been transferred by his Bishop from Water- bury, Connecticut, to Westerby, Rhode Island, as a rebuke' for his connection with Irish politics. In his farewell ad- dress he defended his conduct both as a man and a priest. CAREY'S MIIRDERER.-o'Donnell, the man who shot Jas. Carey, has been committed for trial on the charge of mur- der, and it is believed that he will be arraigned at the Port Elizabeth Assizes in October. In the prisoner's box has been found a woodcut portrait of the notorious "approver." Two Dublin ladies named Wilson were bathing at Bray, when one of them got out of her depth, and being seized with , cramp, was rapidly drowning, when a lady named Whyte, " who was passing, plunged in with her clothes on, ' and, swimming to Miss Wilson, held her until both were 'rescued. THE Inrser NATIONAL LEAGUE.—At a meeting of the Irish National League on Wednesday, in Dublin, Mr. Michael Devitt was elected a member. The week's receipts were announced at £l.lOO, and resolutions were adopted to attend diligently to the registration of voters at the coming revision. Three more of the miscreants who attempted to blow up with dynamite the house ofigr. John Ross Mahon, a Gal- way landlord, have been convicted. Two of them were sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment, and the third. who was one of the ringleaders in the affair, to 10 years' penal servitude. Cardinal M'Cabe he.s addressed a letter to the clergy of Dublin urging prayers for protection from the threatened visitation of cholera, and warning the people against intem- perance and the holding of wakes, which are an outrage upon religion, an insult to the memory of the dead, and powerful allies of contagion. VALUR OF LAND IN TIFPERARY.—A. farm of 112 Irish acres at Balliriahinch, in the county Tipperary, held under lease for thirty-gght years at a rent of £2B-0, reduced by the Land Court to £2OO, has been sold by auction, after a spirited competition, for £930. This is a remarkable fact at a time when so much is said about the deterioration of property. The names of 120 jurors were then called over, and only eleven answered. The fine was imposed in the case of each absentee.
