Her Majesty's Government now poss,ssed fresher news, which enabled them to say with cantidenca that nothing had occurrtd in recent trans- actions which could disturb the frikldlv relations which had now for so long a period subsisted between England and France. In regard to Ireland, the statt, of that country was much more satisfactory than it was at this time last year. There had been a resumption of peace and order, and the dangerous associations which unhappily had exissed had been considerably broken up. He passed a warm enlogium upon Lord Spenser for the firmness and 'rigour with which, during a most trying period, he had administered the affairs of Ireland. Ia regard to the work of the present session he denied that it has been barren of legislation, but he admitted that the progress of domestic reform was slow. This year for the first time the experi- ment of Grand Committees had been tried, and he expressed a hope that the people of the country would watch with deeper interest than ever the working of the machinery of the House cf Commons. He commended the subject to the reflection of every 'intelligent Englishman, because after all the country was a self-governing country, and it was there- fore of the utmost importance that tEe legislative machine should be arranged that necessary and loudly demanded domestic reforms were not brought to an entire standstill by the sheer inability of the two Houses of Parliamept to legis- late.—The Lord Mayor gave "The Houses of Parliament," coupling with the toast the names of the Earl of Kimberley and the Chancellor of the Exchequer, both of whom responded. THE WES LEYAN CONFERENCE. The pastoral sasions of the Wesleyan Conference at Hull closed on Saturday, after a variety of miscellaneous business had been rapidly gone through. It appeared from the report of the Book Committee that the publishing house in London was in a flourishing condition. Tne Huts of deputations from home and "foreign missions were represented, and various official appointments were made. The Rev. Anthony Ward was elected a member of the Legal Hundred in place of the Rev. Edwin Tindall, of Manchester, whose resigna- tion was announced. The Conference in its representative session assembled on Monday. The proceedings commenced with devotional exercises, after which the secretary called over the list of ministerial and lay representatives, and then the President delivered the inaugural actiress, Several notices of motion were given. Hems mission affairs were next taken, which, with the report of the sustentation fund, and the report of the Chapel Committee, occupied the remainder of the session. On Tuesday the President read a long letter from the Rev. T. Jones, Wesleyan missionary at Naples, giving an account of\the terrible earthquake at lechia in which several English Wesleyaps had suffered. It was resolved to inaugu- rate a subscription for their relief. Reports were presented of the South and North Wales _District Chapel funds, and the relief and extension fund for Methodism in Scotland. The report of the Metropolitan Chapel hinds was next taken, and gave rise to discussion. At eleven o'clock business was suspended for the usual conversation on the spiritual con- dition of the various societies throughout Great Britain, which was continugd during the remainder of the session. IThe present condition of Methodism was regarded as most satisfactory, and the zeal and activity of the Church of Eng- land, and other bodies, was spoken of with thankfulness. Business was resumed on Wednesday. A report on the extension of Methodism in Great Britain was taken as read. In moving its adoption Mr. R. W. Perks, of London. referred to the difficulty experienced in obtaining sites for Methodist chapels in the villages, especially in the south of England, owing to the intolerance of a certain class of landlords, and urged that the support of the Connexion should be given to any effort made in Parliameat to give compulsory powers for obtaining sites for places of worship. The affatrs of the ministerial colleges gave rise to a lengthened conversation. A request presented by Dr. Osborn, on behalf of the New South Wales and Queensland Conferences, that 17 additional men be granted, led to an animated debate, which resulted in the applications being granted conditionally. The re- port of the Committee on Connexional and Circuit Finance occupied several hours in consideration. The mode of as- sessment for_the children's fund was changed, and the sum of £27,500 was taken as the amount required to be raised an- nually for the service of the fund during the first five years. At Thursday's meeting a proposal made by Mr. T.'P. Bunting, that the missionary college at Richmond should be given up, Was rejected by the Conference. The schools' fund, the children's fund, and the auxiliary fund were severally passed under review. Educational affairs followed. The conuexional day and Sunday schools were reported to be in a high state of efficiency. There were 842,000 young persons connected with the Sunday schools, an increase of more than 12,000 on the sear, with upwards of 100,000 church members or in junior society classes. The cordial thanks of the Conference were presented to the Mayor of Hull for his reception of the Conference on Wednesday night, which was attended by 1,000 guests, and was highly successful.

MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. The Lerds' Committee on the Ship Canal heard tbe case for the Liverpool Corporation on Saturrday. It was sup- ported by the evidence of Sir W. B. Forwood, who said he was certain that it would be impossible to get ships to go to Manchester at the same rate of freights as to Liverpool. The whole of the gain would be swallowed up three times over if there were any extra freight and insurance to be charged. He would never think of sending a large steamer up the canal—partly on account of the risk and largely on account of the delays. The project seemed to him to be the most visionary scheme ever brought leefore Parliament, and It was not supported by the moneyed classes. The hostile evidence was continued on Monday, engineers of eminence stating their grounds Of difference with the promoters on questions of railway deviation, sufficiency of estimates, probable delays in transit through the canal, if made, and other disputed points.—The London and North. Western Railway Company's chief engineer said the cast of the undertaking was largely under-estimated, and if the proposed railway alterations were carried out danger and difficulty would attend their working. On Tuesday, after untavourable evidence from the general managers of several influential railway companies whose lines are, under the Bill, to be deviated, Mr. Pope, Q C., addressed the Committee in behalf of the London and North- Western and Great Western Companies. He argued that the moneyed classes of Lancashire were not backing the Bill, and that, if it passed, the capital necessary wohld not be raised. The learned gentleman asked, in cenclusion, that the " piece-meal " scheme before their Lordships should be rejected, and the promoters required to ceme forward in another session with plans of a complete and properly I matured undertaking. The opposition of Sir H. de Trafford, the Cheshire Lines Committee, and the Corporation of Birkenhead to the Ship Canal Bill was considered on Wednesday. Mr. Littler (counsel for the Cheshire Lines) asked for a decision ad- versa to the promoters, stating that only one section—and that not the most intelligent or wealthy—of Manchester citizens were in favour of the ache afe. Mr. Adamson, re- called, offered an explanation of his evidence in regard to Mr. Hugh Mason's letter declining to support the bill in Parliament or to lend his name to the agitation. It was at the time a distinct impression on his (Mr. Adamson's) mind, he said, that Mr. Mason declined to " back " the bill in consequence of bang largely interested in the Mersey Docks Board, but on reading the letter afresh he found that he was wrong in that respect; the hon. member holding no shares in that concern. Witness did net previously know that Mr. Mason looked upon the scheme prospectively as a complete failure. • The Committee concluded its labours on Thursday. Nothing remained but the opposition of the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, counsel for which body described the Bill as an innovation on the principles of legislation. Mr. Pember, for the promoters, replied to the arguments and dealt with the adverse evidence offered in babalf of the imrious opposing interests, expressing his con- viction that the bill was needed, and that if 'it passed, the necessary capital would be raised in Lancashire. After a very short consultation in private, the Chairm In announced, as the decision of the Committee, that "it was not expedient to proceed with the bill in the present sO3sion of Parliament." His Lordship signified their high appreciation of the ability and energy with which counsel for the promoters had conducted so arduous a case. Lord Camperdown's announcement to the House of Lords res- pecting the decision on the bill was to the effect that the Select Committee "had decided that it was not expedient to proceed further with the bill."

THE PRINTER'S DEVIL -IX. [By ANGLO-SCOTIIS.] (The right of re-publication is reserved.) The last instalment of these erratic papers of mine, and of which I sin afraid readers of The Examiner must be this time be getting tired, was. devoted to the confusion oi idea or motive suggested by the substituioa of the letters d u for te. Though it has no connection, strictly speaking, with the vagaries of the P.D., an amusing illustration of the confusion arising from the fact of its being possible to spell a family name differently without altering the sound of its pronunciation, may prove interesting to readers of The Examiner, from its lecal associations. As is well known to Lancastrians and Deva Castrians, the family of the East Hall, High Leigh, Cheshire, now represented by the gallant Lieutenant-Colouel Cornwall Legb, spell their name L-e-g-h---without the i. ' The family of the West Hall, now represented by the equally gallant Captain Egerton Leigh, spell their name L-e-i-g-h. In 1879 the difference in spelling was pungently and wittily bit (.4f bysthe Rev. A. J. Richardson, as follows : If h Tisetaet came os n a it tatevoisfthpiresgreshatte to haictastHrainggherLewighoul;d see, To his mind it would cause great confu.lon and bother, To find things so mix'.l up he one with the other: Two Estabistiments separate. two Halls, and two Squires, Two parsons, two chapels, two bells, and two choirs Whilst the magnates themselves couldn't fdirly agree As to spelling correctly the nameof " Jfl h Ltigh One stoutly insisting o i with the e, The other on nothing between e and g ; On map and on sign-post you'd meet with ilk-, i, P.0.0.'s were without it, and folks wondered why' Then the agent found out, wh,unre took the big ledger down, The estates all mix'd up with the farms of Lord Egerton' And directions for letters and parcels were wrapt lii A regular muddle 'twat Colonel and Captain ; For if to " The Hail" they should chance be address'd, It was doubtful if meant for the " East " or the" West;" But for rights or precedence 'twas doubtful which had 'ern, For neither could trace up much briber than Adam ! So what you're about, be particular, please. For Meatus e is full of cats, cheeses, ant Leighs, Leghs of Lyme, Leghs of Adlington. everything" Logo," From the inuerm st bounds to the hant:s of the Dee; And from dropping a letter what comes there's rso Bo you'd best mind yc•ur i, and look atter your spailin . The lines are to be found reprinted this year in No. 6 of the Manchester Ocai.terly. To get back to the old track, and to deal with a somexhat similar case of transposition as that touched upon in No. 8, I may as well relate that Mr Spencer Vincent was the other day described as the" Chief of the Criminal Legislature Department,"—" legislature" being substituted for "investigation" by the printer. In the same paper the description of the doings of a "vague elephant', no doubt puzzled readers. Of course a rogue elephant was meant. The "largest quadrupeds" are certainly far front, being" vague" in any sense of the word, although many of the dictionaries are hazy in their references to the animal's so-called trunk. The word "trunk" is a corruption of the old English name "trump," which was correctly derived from the Latin. Pliny says" the elephant can make a noise like a trumpet,"—hence the name " trump," which the French still retain (la trompe). The rendering of the poetical sentiment " He kissed her under the silent stars;' tieing translated by the compositor into "lie kicked her under the cellar stairs," is stereotyped; but " Bonds for violent kinds of spectres," for " Bands at the violent end of the spectra,"is not an altogether unfacetious or inharmonious stroke or vibration on the gamut of " cord' and" colour." But perhaps the lees said about cords the better. To skip from science to art. " Her Daughter's Leg's off," was the interpretation one Caxtonian gave to the title of the pathetic picture which represents an aged dame ter.derly lifting the baby of her daughter, recently dead, from the cot or cradle in which the little orphan has re Idled the sorrow-stricken grandmother. Possibly the writer of the art criticism in which the mistake Occurs terminates some of his words rather indistinctly, and so "Leg's off" duly appeared instead of Legacy. In an American journal, the other day, the well-known Soule Photograph Coinpany of Boston came out in print as the "Soul Photographic • Company." The compositor no doubt believed with Young in the realistic existence of "That hideous sight, a naked human heart." Or, if he agreed with Mrs. Barbanld in her aasertion that, "Souls are ripened in our northern sky," he had an idea that they could be photographed,like cereals, roots, flowers, or fruit; and, if need be; coloured by band afterwards. " Berry funny," as the nigger would say, is the following :—" Where it is a question ot the choice of evils, a bigamous marriage is hated more than an Eastern harem."' And no doubt there are a geod many male persons of the- same opinion as the compositor who, in setting up the sentence, substituted the words " hated more" for "better." Even in its correct form most people will dis— sent from the opinion expressed. To men of a romping dis-- position, a "high old time with the girls "would no doubt, be more acceptable than the " two years' hard," and the diet too plentifully leavened with skilly, that usually attends aggravated cases of double marrying; but sensible men will . agree with ms that here in England an extra wife is an un- desirable superfluity, to say nothing of a " collection " of wives. Let me earnestly advise Nervtonians to refrain from the lesser as well as the major evil, at all events, until the English marriage laws are more nearly assimilated to those of the Burmese, who can pretty well dissolve the marriage contract at will. And even the Burman jests at the ta-koo-lat, or divorcee : "She that's neither maid, married, nor widow, Fits all mem as a pot does its lid, 0." Talking of Burmese marriage-lore, the rhynie of the, ran-hpot (the hostile pai:s) freely translated is as fol- ,ows

"Friday's daughter Didn't oughter Marry with a Moacl,y's son; Should she do it, She will rue it, Life's last lap will so,n be run." Fowl pas sit, if Monday's son-married two or more of Ft idav'E daughters, I presume sudden death would ensue. If it didn't, it ought to. Man should not be greedy in the matter of wives, seeing that the mere fact of a woman covet- ing such a paltry thing as an apple—(and for anything we know,that might bavz been sour and given her the stomach- ache)—has up to now brought about so much mischief.

div.head: COAL MINING IN LANCASHIRE.
div.p: COAL MINING IN LANCASHIRE.

The reports of the Inspectors of Mines for North, East, and West Lancashire have just been issued, and Contain same interesting information relative to mining pursuits in these districts in 1882. The quantity of coal raised in North and East Lancashire during the year was '9,749,36?- tons, and in West Lancashire 10,031.282 tons. rile number of persons employed in the North and east districts (which are under the inspection of Mr. J. Dickinson) was 26,125, of whom 23,354 were over 16 years of age; 2,255 ranged. from 13 to 16 years, aud 339 from 12 to 13 years of age. These were employed under ground. There were also ein- ployed :above ground 5,482, of whom 226 were females and 4,783 males. The total employed above and below ground was 31,607. In the West Lancashire district 24,505 per- sons were employed under ground, and of these 22,409 were over 16 years of age. 5,892 I).rsoris were employed above ground ; giving a total above and below ground of 30,397. During ths year the number of sepa- rate fatal accidents in North and East Lancashire wile 63. In West Lancashire and North Wales there were 93 senarate fatal accidents, and 95 lives were lost. In Mr. Dickinson's report he observes that during the last nine, years the number of youths under 16 years who were cw- ployed in learning the practical business of coal-mining in that district has diminished fre;nt 4,474 to 2,771. A table which is appended to the report shows that there were 04- ployed in the mines of North and East Lancashire in 1874 27,166 persons of all ages. of whom 22,692 were above 16 years of age; whilst in 1882 the number was 26,125. From 13 to 16 years of age there were 3,184 employed in 1874., against 2,255 in 1882; and in the same years the number between 12 anl 13 years of age shows a still farther decrease, there being in 1814 1.012 employed, whilst last year the number has fallen to 339. In noting the number of females employed about the colleries of West Lancashire Mr. Hall says "the occupation of these women is somewhat rough,and they are often exposed to all kinds of weather, yet they generally look strong and healthy, and in this respcct certainly have the advantage of those engaged in factories." The inspector observes that there has been a remarkable alrence of explosions of fire-damp in the district during the wear, only three persons having lost their lives from this Cause, whilst nearly 13 000,000 tons of minerals have been produced from the mines.

LOCAL TAXATION IN LANCASHIRE AND CHESIIIRE.—From an interesting paper just issued by the Statistical Depart- ment, giving the average amount expended upon each pauper out of the poor rates, including everything connected with their maintenance, it seems that in Lancashire the average cost per head of paupers for maintenance on all expenses connected therewith was £lO 4s 6d; the total amount ex- pended being .2753 957 ; the average cost per head of the population being 4s 7tal. The amount expended for pur- poses totally unconnected with relief amounted to £ll 7s SA-d per bead, of paupers receiving relief, the total being £838,424; the average of the same per head of the popula- tion was 4s 91.1. The cost of the police out of the poor rates amounted to £8 8s Bid per head of paupers, and 33 61,1 per head of the population the total cost teeing £621,860. The average cost of the Officers and their rations per had of paupers was £1 Gs 2±,1, the total being £106,598. The remaining portion of the poor rates are given to local authorities, school boards, etc.—ln Cheshire the average cost per head of paupers lor maintenance and all purposes con- nected therewith was £9 3s 71d, the total amount expended being £137,173. The average cost per head of the popula- tion was 4s 4id. The average cost per pauper for monies expended for purposes totally unconnected with relief to the poor was £l3 2s 9d, the total being £186,131; the average cost of the same per head of the population was 5s 11td. The average cost of the police per head of paupers was £7 178 SP, the total being £111,547, being an average cost of 3s 7d per head of the population. The average cost of the officers and rations per head of the paupers receiving relief was £1 63 2t, the total cost being £18,593. MANCHESTER, WARRENOTON, PRnSCO r, AND LIVERPOOL, IN 1760.—The subjoined notice of several towns in South Lancashire is extracted from the letters of an antiquary who visited the county in July, 1760. The letters were printed many years afterwards in The Gentleman's Magazine. The reference to Manchester shows that in 1760 a place of 30,000 inhabitants was regarded as being "a prodigious large town ":—" Manchester is a prodigious large town; contains 30,000 inhabitants, four churches, and ten chapels of ease; yet is but one parish, which reaches nine miles round : the largest part of it is new and well built, consisting of the dwellings and warehouses of the traders, who deal in f us- tians, tapes, ticking, and checks. On the 26th [July] I came to Warrington, where there is a famous manufactory of huckabeck pins (which are sold for 2s. 4d. a pound), glass, and copper. There is alto tneeting[i.e. Dissenters' chapel] and an Icademy,kept by Dr. Tayior,of dorwich,who has two or three professors under him, all in very handsome houses. Thence I went to Prescot, where is a greet pottery; and on Saturday to Liverpool, where I spent Sunday. It is a hand- some town, but rather dirty, by the number of sailors in the trade. The River Mersey lies at the back of the town, and Ills the decks, which are very large, and full of ships. Tisere have beers several batteries erected last year [1759] for fear of the French fleets; and they are going to make more. On Sunday morning, about 10 o'clock, a Greenland ship came in, and fired seven guns as a signal that she had taken so many whales, and was saluted by the bells of the princi- pal church; this was an agreeable entertainment; and when service was over, I walked down to the dock to see her. I returned to Warrington yesterday, and am now on my way home across Cheshire and Staffordshire. The Cheshire roads are very deep in dust, and the middle paved like London streets, but through a fine cultivated country, though the towns do not stand at all thick."

THE LANCASHIRE IRON AND COAL TRADES.—There was less than-the average attendance on 'Change at Manchester, on Tuesday, and business operations had evidently only partially recovered from the interruption caused by the holidays. Prices, however, continue very steady, and although inquiries are on an extremely small scale buyers are unable to obtain any concessions from makers, who in most cases are still kept so well employed with deliveries against the contracts they have in hand that they are in- different about booking further orders except at, their full rates. Occasional orders are secured by Lancashire pig iron makers at their list rates of 45s to 45s 6d, less 2, for forge and foundry qualities delivered equal to Manchester, and these are sufficient to take away any surplus output beyond their deliveries. In district brand makers are generally so fully sold that in some cases there is a disposi- tion to stiffen upon the minimum figures of 44s 10d to 45s 10d less 2 for forge and foundry Lincolnshire delivered here, but it can scarcely be said that business is being done at advanced rates. For manufactured iron there is a mode- rate demand at about £6 2s 6d to £6 5s for bars, £6 12s 6d for hoops, and £8 7s 6d for sheets delivered into this dis- trict. The reduction in the wages of the finished iron warkers, which led to the strike in Staffordshire, has now been put in force throughout this dis- trict. The demand for shipment continues only quiet.— Business in the coal trade of this district continues to move on very steadily for the season of the year. Colliery pro- prietors are able to maintain their prices, and the pits are kept running on an average of four to five days a week, with comparatively very little of the output going into stock. Both house-fire and common_ classes of round coal meet with a fairly good sale, the demand for shipment, which has bean tolerably brisk of late, taking away in a large measure any surplus supplies left over from home trade requirements, and generally there is an almence of that pressure- to sell which is usual during the summer months. The general feeling in the market is that the next movement in prices will be in an upward direction, and this causes a pressure on the part of buyers to purchase for forward delivery, but in many cases colliery proprietors decline altogether to com- mit themselves to forward engagements, and where they are prepared to contract it is only at advanced rates. Slack is moving off rather better than of late, but is still plentiful in the market, and all through the summer this class of fuel has been difficult to deal with, the common sorts being quite a drug. At the pit mouth prices remain as under ;—Best coal, 9s; seconds, 7s; common, 63 6d to 6s; burgy, 4s 6d to ss; best slack, 4s to 4s 3d ; and common sorts as to 3s 6d per ton; delivered at Garston or Liverpool steam coal averages 7s 3d to 7s 9d, and seconds house coat about Si Oil per ton.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, AUGUST 11, 1883.

Ministers dined with the LORD MAYOR at the Mansion House on Wednesday evening, and it will be generally admitted that the hos- pitable gathering in the present instance has taken place under most favourable circurn- stances to the Administration. The fourth session of the present Parliament is nOW drawing to a close, yet the influence of the Government has in no way diminished, they have still a solid majority at their back, and amongst their supporters there is every con- fidence that the PREMIER and his colleagues will yet add materially to the great measures of Reform which in 1880 the constituencies returned them to power to accomplish. There is peace abroad, and there is not now any- thing which can be foreseen likely to upset our amicable relations with foreign powers; Irish grievances having been removed, there is no burning questions which disturb the even tenour of our ways at home; and with a good and abundant harvest in prospective there is combined a feeling of thankfulness and contentment on all 'hands. These are elements which contribute to make a gather- ing such as that of Wednesday something more of a pleasure than it would otherwise be. Interest on these occasions centres chiefly in the utterances of the PRIME MINISTER. In this instance he had no startling dis- closures to make, and if we except his state- ment respecting the Madagascar incident he had nothing new to tell. That incident, as we all know, created a most painful sensation in this country. but it was never for a moment supposed that it would lead to any rupture of the good feeling which has so long existed between the two nations. It seemed ap- parent from the first that the indiscretion of the French Admiral could be, without much difficulty, satisfactorily explained; and though we never feared any serious complications, it is a relief to read the state- ment of the head of the Government that a full and ample explanation has been given by France, and that he feels " confident no- thing will arise out of these transactions that can disturb the long accord between England' and France, which has now survived an anxious and interesting struggle." It is highly creditable to the diplomatists of both countries that these irritating episodes can be arranged without recourse to any hostile demonstration. The PREMIER'S speech was, robbed of much of the interest which shoula have attached to it but for his statement ifl the House of Commons on 2,londay respecting- Egypt, coupled with the subsequent' communication on the same subject froa Lord DUFFERIN, the contents of which Mr., GLADSTONE made known on ruesday. there was one thing more than another upon which the country desired to know the inten- tions of the Government it was undoubtedif their views upon the Egyptian question. is now nearly twelve months since the Egyptian war, we have been in occupation. of the country ever since, during that WO. Ministers have made declarations to the-effec that it was not intended by the Governalatt: that the occupation should be permanent, ye' there was no sign of the withdrawal of our troops. In August of last year Mr. GLAD"' STONE stated that of all things in the world we were not going to occupy Egypt for an in- definite time, whilst in the spring of this yeo Lord HARTINGTON said that six montb! represented with probable accuracy the length of time that it might be necessary to keep our troops in that country. The period of months has now very nearly expired, still the occupation continues. Nothing, of course', would please the Opposition better than thag' the Government should declare their intentio.° to occupy Egypt for ever—that is the Oplwslo" tion policy, yet they would be the first t, condemn the government if they changeu their views and proposed an indefinite occu: pation ; on the other hand, if the Governrnen.; were to scuttle out of Egypt at once, °cll. would present a favourable opportunity i° - the Opposition raising a cry that the Govern ment had failed—inasmuch as tne reconsti.tun- tion of Egypt is not yet on a safe foundat,, —to carry out their promises towards to, Egyptians. The Opposition are not to 100, are gratified, for the occupation is, we alact , _ to learn, only to confirm until it is felt tnrA

HORRIBLE ASSAULT AT RUNCORN. Runcorn is gaining an unenviable notoriety on account of the dastardly assaults which are taking place there. Re- ceutly two men have been sentenced to long terms of incar- ceration for conduct of a most vile nature with girls who are mere children, and at the Police Court, on Wednesday, Mr. W. Bankes was occuped in hearing another cay. ft details of which were most harrowing. The victim of the man's lustful passion is a girl named Mary Jane Ellis, w1:0 is 11 years of age, and lives with her parents in Wiverne place, Runcorn, where the prisoner, who is a married man. 42 years of age, with a wife and one child, also lives. He was placed in the dock, having been apprehended on a war- rant, to answer a charge of criminally assaulting the girl, although at one time it was feared that he would have to meet a more serious accusation. The evidence adduced was utterly unfit for publication, but it may be stated that on on Saturday evening the prisoner met the girl on the Mallet ground, and induced her to walk with him down Irwell-lx„-:e to a secluded spot near the 01 Quay Mills. Here he held a disgusting conversation with the girl, and acted in a re- volting manner, seriously injuring his victim.—lie was wremanded until to-day (Saturday).

take the earliest opportunity of returning to poli- tical life, and will be found among the candidates for Scotch constituencies at the next general election. With the end of this month Mr. John Morleyie con- neetion with the Pall Mall Gazette comes. He not only withdraws from the editorship, tut, I under stand, will not continue as a contributor. It is not improbable that we shall see some new departure iq ' the Pall Hall when Mr. -Morley retires. I don't mean that it will be any less Liberal than at present, but there may be points of policy on which Mr. Mor- ley would differ, and therefore his severance from the journal will be final and complete. This will be a great, even an irreparable, loss to English journalism. There are many things Mr. John Morley has done well, but nothing so useful as the uplifting of the Pall Mall Gazette to its present position. This was a, task the difficulty of which can only be fully appre- eiated by those engaged in the direction of journsls. Mr. Greenwood, who originally made the Pall Mall Gazette, and at one time endowed it with wide public influence, was leaving to start another journal. The Pall Mall itself was turning round from a position of strong, almost hysterical, Toryism to the broadest Liberalism. It would. certainly lose all its former readers, and the question was whether it would gain a sustaining circle of new ones? Mr. Morley speedily settled that point. He made a journal which is a marvel of good editing, and which in its editorial department had a freshness and in- dependence striking by contrast with some of its contemporaries. In some senses the politieal influence of the Pall Mall Gazette under Mr. Morley's direction has been greater than that of any Eaglish journal, not excepting the Times. The Times of course has a wider range, and it appeals to a class of people born in a kind of religious belief in its infallibility. Bat in the House of °ominous, amongst men who really govern the nation, the Pall Mall Gazette held, and now holds, a higher position. Mr. litlorloy's abdication of the direction of this influence is, I believe, inspired by a desire to devote himself to p ilitical life. He has had many years of journalism, and thinks he has done enough. He will not be absolutely lost to the profession, since he will shortly undertake the editor- ship of a new sixpenny monthly magazine. In the meantime, as soon as Parliament is up, he is going to Switzerland for a period of much-needed rest. Mr. Sims Reeves has been making up his accounts, and has come to the conclusion that he ought to be £75,000 richer than he is. This mere trifle of balance arises out of the necessity, frequently imposed upon him by the state of his health, of either abandoning engagements when they have been undertaken, or declining to enter upon fresh ones. He never knows when he gets up in the morning whether he will be able to sing at night, so delicate is his throat. But, apart from these losses, be has done pretty well dur- ing the forty years he has been singing. When a man gets £6OO for a night's work, as Mr. Reeves has done before now at the Birmingham Festival, it is not necessary that he should work six days a week.
FATAL ACCIDENT TO A BOY AT WIDNES.

Yesterday, John Burns, 10 years of age son of James Burns, living at 13, Viaduct-street, was killed at Messrs. Golding and Davies works, Widnes Marsh, Widnes. At noon the boy was sent to the works with his father's 'dinner, 'which he safely delivered. la returning home he walked along a line of waggons in the yard; and wishing to get to the other side, he stepped in an opening which he descried in them. At that instant the engine moved the waggons, and the poor boy's head was caught between the buffers and fearfully crushed. He died half an hour after- wards, and his dead body was conveyed homa. The coroner has been warned of the sad occurrence.

SAD SUICIDE OF A RUNCORN MAN. Mr. Joseph Harper, marine store dealer, Runcorn, com- mitted suicide oq Sunday evening last. For some time past the deceased had been in a despondent state of mind in con- sequence of the depression in the particular trade in which he was engaged, and he has frequently expressed a wish that lee was dead. On Sunday afternoon, however, be was unusually cheerful, and promised to take his children to Overton Hills en Bank Holiday. His trouble still pdadjeased its hold upon his mind, for he remarked that as he 6414 no money they would have to walk, following the observation with a laugh. After tea Harper, according to his custom, went into his office, which was opposite his residence in Water-street, in order, it was supposed, to attend to his book-keeping and correspondence. Seven o'clock arrived, and he was still there. Suspicions Wine.' anused, a man named Peter O'Neil entered the store, and discovered the unfortunate man hanging by a hempen rope to a beam. He was at once cut down, and Or. Robinson was sent for, but that gentleman's services were not required, as life was quite extinct. Overturned on the floor near the spot where the deceased was hanging was an office stool. Upon this Harper had evi- dently stood whilst he fastened the rope to the beam, and the loose noose round his neck, and than jumped off, strangu- lation quickly ensuing. It has been stated that the only money found since the sad aff iir amounts to ss. 41. A juryman at the inquest ouserVed that some time ago he saw the deceased's bank book, and there was then to his credit at Parr's Bank the sum of £Boo.—Mr. Ridgway, of War- rington, held an inquest on the body on Tuesday, when the jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased com- mitted suicide whilst temporarily insane.
BANK ilk .IY. RUNCORN.

In Itativrn Bank lloliday was very•generally observed, the tradespeople, with few exceptions,. closing their places of business. Up to noon the streets presented a very dull and deserted aspect, rain, which commenced in the early morning, desceadiug in an unceasing shower, which made pleasure in the open air impossible. Towards one o'clock, however, the dark grey clouds which had hidden the sky rolled away, the cup sent forth its genial rays, and every- thing quickly bore an aspect more consonant with the mid- summer solstice. Pleasure-seekers could be seen wending their way to the railway station in parties of two, three, and four, no less than 300 persons being booked to Frodsham by the 2-15 trait!, while a further 300 were booked during the afternoon: Liverpool and Chester were also visited by great numbers of Runcornians. The workmen of Messrs. Brun- drit and Co. joined the Widnes Parish Church excursion, which passed through the town in the morning for Llan- dudno, WIDNES. _ _

Holidays, ba they conn-ee-t-e-i;vith the Bank or an ecclesi- astical festival, are always welcomed by the hardy toilers in the chemicil centre,•whose labour is uncongenial, and whose surroundings are to a great extent not picturesque but squalid. Monday was no exception to the rule, and the majori,y of the Widnesians had deserted their furnaces and evaporating pans for the green fields and the sea side. True the weather in the morning was most unpromising, and rain descended with a persistency that seemed destined toi last through the day, hut notwithstanding this fact 800 persons left the town for Llandudno and Rhyl by the Widnes Parish Church excursion, and spent a most enjoyable day amid the lovely Welsh scenery. At the present time, how- ever, Widnes is suffering rather severely from depression in the chemical trade, several of the firms having recently reduced the number of their workmen, and in consequence the exodus of the inhabitants was scarcely so marked as on previous holidays. On both lines of railway the traffic was heavy, Liverpool and Manchester being visited by large num;ers, especially in the afternoon, when the weather was beautifully fine. -

The CLERK read a letter which Mr. W. Handley had re- ceived from the treasurer of Liverpool Infirmary, stating that five guineas was the customary subscription from Unions to the Hospital.—The CLERK remarked that since 1876 six patients had been sent to Manchester Infirmary, an average of one per year. This year they had sent two.— Mr. WEIR gave notice that at the next meeting he would move that the resolution passed at the last meeting be rescinded, and that the subocription tie contributed to the Manchester Infirmary.

STATE OF THB HOUSE. The Master reported that 78 men and 93 women had been relieved during the past wrek. The were 176 inmates in the house as compared with 153 in the corresponding period last year. Thirty boys and 23 girls were in attendance at school, and eight girls were receiving industrial training. Four vagrants had been relieved during the week. The water necessary for the carrying on of the work of the Vul- can ironfoundry has hitherto been obtained from one or two pits in the neighbourhood, but so low and email did the supply becsme that the firm were compelled to stop a large number of the hands on Wednesday week. Since that time the whole of the forgemen have been disengaged, although the tirin have had several pressing orders *o complete, An d they could ill afford to stop the men. Arrangements are being made by which it is hsped that a similar difficulty wal net be met with in future.

div.head: SONS OF TEMPERANCE.
div.p: SONS OF TEMPERANCE.

EUNCORN BR ATICH. The members of the Runcorn branch of the Sons sf Temperance held their annual demonstrations on Sunday and Monday last. en the former day the members, veha number, all told, about 250, assembled in the Devonshire. squire shortly after one o'clock, and a successful meeting was held, Messrs. Withington, Faulkner, and S. Timperley delivering addresses. They then walked in procession to Bsthesda Chapel, which bad been kindly lent for the occa- sion. An interesting service was gone through, the choir, under the leadership of Mr. Fairhurst, rendering music ap- propriate to the occasion; and the Rev. J. D. Thomas preached an eloquent sermon in support of teetotalism. Monday opened with a dull grey sky, from which rain heavily descended at intervals during the forenoon, and the prospects for the out-door proceedings of the Sons of Tem- aerance were anything but reassuring. Noon past, however, and the weather brightened considerably. At two o'clock, when the members of the Order commenced their parade from Regent-street school-room, the sun was brilliantly shining. Heading the procession wee two mounted marshalls—Mr. Jones and Mr. Heesom—followed by the Mill Brow brass band. The splendid banner of the branch, which has just been obtained at considerable expense, was next in position, and it attracted much attention from the the spectators who assembled in the streets to view the demonstration. On one side is represented a life boat, manned by a sturdy crew, who are impelling it over the stormy waters to the rescue of the sufferers on a wreck. On the reverse is a beautiful painting of the emblem of the Order Holding the cords of the banner were fouryoung ladies—the Misses Withington, Miss Stringer, and Miss West—while charmingly dressed young girls, named Misses Birch, Clarke, Henderson, and Ridge, held the streamers. The adult members, 160 in number, faulted, wearing badges, their rear being brought up by the Weston brass band, who led the members of the Weston division and the juvenile section, numbering about 100. Then came the life boat drawn on a lurry kindly lent by Mr. John Moores. It was manned by a crew of boys (dressed in handsome senor costume) consisting of John Faulkner coxswaine, S. Brown, W. Faulkner,.W.Santley, T. Wilson, and W. Cooke. Standing on the four corners of the lorry, which was decorated with coloured cloth, embellished with appropriate mottoes, were Masters Boyle, Inglesfield, and brothers Faulkner. From Devonshire-square the procession wended its way to the residence of Mr. T. Norman, in theenway-road, where the bands played a selection; then by Shaw-street, Waterloo Bridge, Ashbridge- street, Dukes-field, Lord-street, and Church-street, to the residence of Dr. Robinson, the surgeon to the Order. The band again gave a selection, and then by way of King-street, Bridge-street, and Halton-road,Crane was visited, a stoppage being made at the Rev. George Hack's residence, where more music was discoursed. From here the procession proceeded to a field kindly lent by Mr. Astbury. The weather was now all that could be desired, and a variety of games were entered into with much zest. After the bands had played for Mr. Asthury's delectation, the members returned to Regent-street schoolroom, calling on the way at the residences of Mrs. Lea and Dr. Mac- Dougall (surgeon of the Weston division), in High-street. At five o'clock tea was provided in Bethesda Schoolroom. Large demands were made upon the accommodation pro- vided, over 300 persons sitting down to the repast. The tables were presided over by Miss Hedlington, Mrs. Cooke, Mrs. James Taylor, Miss Withington, Miss Stringer Mrs. Wilson, Mrs. Edgar, Mrs. Gibson, Mrs. Lacey, Mrs. Treacy, Mrs. Bisbrown, Mrs. Heesom, Mrs. Jones, and Mrs. Corker. Subsequently a snost successful public meeting was held, the room being crowded to its utmost capacity, whilst many persons were unable to gain admission. Mr, T. Norman occupied the chair, and he wee supported on ' the platform by the Revs. George Hack and J. D. Thomas, Messrs. D. Bisbrown, T. Cooke, W. Heatherington, C. Littler, J. Halford, J. Timperley, Lindon, L Heesoin, Henderson, J. Jones, M. Jones, J. Faulkner, W. Norman, Whitehead, Lacey, W. Cooper, Ackerley, and Williams. Prayer having been opened by the Rev. George Hack, the CHAIRMAN opened the proceedings by a suitable speech, in ' which he remarked the longer lie lived the more he saw the propriety of every man, woman, and child becoming teetotal, aria be urged temperance men not to rest upon the magnifi- cent achievemerits they had already made; but to continue to work earneetly and devoutedly. (applause.)—Mr. COOKE, the secretary, who was warmly greeted, read the annual report of the division. He said the work of the past year had been very encouraging. The Order had never wirnesscil a more prosperous year, and many districts which had been at a standstill had breathed with new life. During the year 33 new divisions and 13 cadet sections had been ioetituted, while there had been an increase of seine 1,500 in the number of the members—(applause)--and a financial increase of £5,465 lOs 3d. (Applause.) The total number of members was now 17,200, and the total fund £53,465 lOs 31. (Applauze.) They inietit form some estimate of the nod influence of the society by the fact, tied during the past year the amount paid in sick claims was over £11,000; and iu death claims, £2280 lied been paid, and nearly £3OO given to deserving members in distress. (Ap- plause ) Who could estimate the value the society had proved in relieving the members? The lifeboat crew divi- sion, the report stated, had now 220 members in good stand- ing, 70 lieving been initiated during the past year. The amount received in contributions was £240, and paid to sick members £l3l 63. Si. £44 had also been paid in death claims, in addition to which the divis'on had retained the cum of 3s. per member, and had sent to the central fund the sum of £2O. (Applause.) The Rev. GEOROE HACK observed that it was the duty of every husband to provide if be possibly could for the future sickness and distress of himself and family, and by the Order of the Sons of Temperance ho could make that provi- sion. But the Order also contemplated the high work of making drunken people sober. In order to accomplish this object, the rev. gentleman pointed out that there must be p ofound conviction, and earnest endeavour, and he re- lited personal incidents to encourage the members in their labour.—ln an excellent speech, Mr. FAULKNER referred to the stripendoas obstacles which the pioneers of teetotalism managed by their zeal to onercome, deducing fruitful lessons for temperance workers of the present day, and lie concluded by enumerating some of the advantages offered by member- ship in the Order of Sons of Temperance —On the motion of the Rev. J. D. Thomas seconded by Mr. LITTLER, a hearty vote of thanke was accorded to the chairman; and a similar and deserved compliment was paid to the ladies who had presided at the tea tables and otherwis • aesis ed in the day's p!oceedines, on the motion of Mr. S. TIMPERLEY seconded by Mr. 13ovan.—During the evening, the band rendered eeveral selections of music in good style. Mr. John Mil- ford, Mr. George Lacey, and Mr. Robert Moores contributed songs which were well received; Mr. George Williams recited "The merry men of England" ; Miss Clark, a vary young girl, sang a hymn in charming style, while Miss 'Clough piesided at the pisno.

THE FATALITY IN A WELL AT WIDNES. Mr. T. W. Barker, the coroner, held an inquest at the Arch lintel, on Saturdav, touching the death of rrederick Wright, who was killed at Messrs. Hall and Shaw's works, on Thursday, whilst engaged in sinking a well. Mr. It Manley was the foreman of the jury. Mr. J. Johnson was present on behalf of Messrs. Halt and Shaw. —William Proffitt, of 16, Oakland-street, a labourer, gave evidence to the effect that the deceased was helping to deepen an old well. He found the deceased with his head in the water and his feet above the surface. lie was quite dead. Wit- ness did not feel the influence of any gas whilst in the well. His opinion of the accident was that the deceased, in coming te the top, had struck his, head against some staging and been stunned.—Thomas Tennant, labeurer, in the employ of Mr. Chap.nan, of Salford, stated he was working about twelve feet from the deceased. The deceased, who had been to the bottom of the well, fell suddenly down when he had been hoisted to within a few feet of the top. He was twelve feet from the staging, and therefore could not have struck it. Witness believed the deceased lived at Salford, and had heard he was twenty-five years of age, and lodged in Church-street, Widnes.—Inspector Barnett . said the wife of the deceased was ill, and owing to the shortness of the notice the police had been unable to get any of his relations to identify him.—Witness, in answer to the 1 Coroner, said he had never heard any of the men complain , of gas in the well.—Mr. Schofield (a juryman): Is it your opinion that he fell through being overcome with gas,— Witness could not express a certain conviction, but he was quite sure that it was not a blow that caused the deceased to fall.—The Coroner : Then it must have been either gas or a sudden attack of illness.—Mr. Johnson remarked that Mr.l Chapman was deepening the well by contract, and Messrs. 'dell and Shaw had nothing to do with it.—The Coroner said the contractor ought to be represented, and as they eauld not get the evidence of an important witness, and the Inspector of Factories was not present, he advised the adjournment of the inquest, which after some discussion I was done. The adjourned inquiry was held on Thursday before Mr. Barker, the coroner. The Government Inspector had writ- ten to say that he should be unable to attend. Mr. Chap- man was present. The first witness, Charles Oldcroft, who said he was engaged at the well, stated that it was the duty of the deceased to steady the boring bar. Deceased did not complain of bad air in the well, but called out "Pull up," and witnesa wound bins up. He came up riding on the boring bar which was a safe thing to do, and, his hands were round the rope. Ha did not cry out before befell. Witness stopped the bar and called out for assistance. A man named liner went down to try and rescue Wright, but when near the bottom he fell oil the " hares," by which lie was decending. Kiltier wis ..lruck by something, but after- wards got on the bar again, and was wound up in a setni-

conscious state. iYittieiti took KiioEr to his lodgings. Atte an hour's sleet) he came Stinted. Before Kilner was taken away Wright was brought to the surface. Witness had not heard any of the workmen complain of gas in the well. Re had wori.ed there about a fortaight.—AJoryman : Why was not the well examined after deceased bad ben down an hour and come up P—Witness : It was deceased's duty to e:t itnine it.—Jurytnan : Have you no means of testing it ? Witness: Yes, we try it by a candle, and had done so several times that day.—Henry Kilner, of Swinton, blJekseuith, in service of Chapman, went down the well a day or two before the accident for otout an hour, and felt all to be right. There was no gas. He went down to find deceased, and after being lowered into water up to his shouldcTs be said "Hold,' and lon cnascieusness. Did not recover until -found himeelf at hie lodgings—Coroner: Was it foul air, do you think, that turned you off in this way ?—Wite ne,s: it must 'a' been that or summat.—John Kilner, 11r1 Everton-road, Longsight, foreman for Chapman, said deceased thoroughly understood his work. Each day two lighted candles were sent cl.iwn the well before the Men to see if the gas was pure or not. Deceased has been with them 21 years. He had been 20 years at the work.—Mr. John- son: There was another man there named Tennant, but he declined to go down—probably for prudential reasons.— The Coroner: What do you think was the c.aase of de- ceased falling ?—Witness: I think he was struck with gas a-ed ceased breathing. The boring itselt would eliminate gasi.—Mr. Johnson: They were not deepening the well, but waning a new boring.—Mr. Lewis (juryman): There was another old boring close to, and that may have liberated some.gas.—Witness : We were boring through material con- sisting of bricks and mortar.—Hannah Elizt Wright, Crane.. street, Ardwick, said she was only married to the deceased on the I7th February last. She had known him two years before that. He was not troubled with dizziness oriainting fits of any kind. He never made any complaint about the way in which the work was managed.—Mr. John Johnson, manamer at works, also gave evidence. Deceased was found to have fallen headfirst. He did not think there was gas in the well. His theory was that the man was seized with sudden faintness, or, having on indiarubber boots, they might have slipped from under him, and precipitated him into the well. —The Coroner thought there must have been an escape of vs.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

Tag HALTON DRAINAGE AGI7ATION. The Cuati remarked that at a recent nieetine,i. Cie rate- payers uf 1-faltuti, it had been stated that ha said at the last meeting of the Authority. that it was entirely' t.‘e (suit of the overseers that the sewage scheme bad been carried out, and that the eatepayers had not been informed a the matter. The Cferk thought those members who were present, would remember that when he was asked if it was the fanit of the overseers, he absolutely declined to say whose fault it was. He read a letter dated May 24th, from Mr. Thomas Wright, the senior overseer of Halton, who, in replying to an invi- tation from Mr. Farrington to attend a meeting of the Committee on the scheme, asked to be excused attendance, as he had had a great deal to do with such like matters in Halton, and was sorry to say generally indeed very un- pleasantly.—At the invitation of the Clerk, the INSPECTOR narrated all the circumstances which led to the adoption of the scheme, which was suggested by Mr. Evans, the agent to Sir Richard Brooke. The Inspector had received the following letter from Mr. J. H. Salkeld, of Runcorn, on behalf "of the trustees :" —"Dear Sir,—We are told there is being made some ex- tensive arrangements for cowering several lots of property at Halton, and that the cost of the sewer will fall upon the ratepayers. We beg to point out that to save putting the town to the expense, and at your suggestion, we spent £5O or £6O in sewering our property at Halton, and we shall certainly feel ourselves aggrieved if other parties can have their work done at the expense of the ratepayers, of whom we are amongst the heaviest." The Inspector remarked that this letter was marked private, but he considered the contents of a public nature, and therefore he had read it. He had replied to the effect that the Authority was responsible for the nuisance, and it was imperative that a sewer should be provided. In doing so the Authority had arranged that the whole of the houses on the line of the sewer could be connected therewith, aad, further, it would be capable of extension to the whole village. IMPORTANT SEWERAGE SCHEME FOR FRODSHAM.

The Frodsham Sewerage Committee reported that they held a meeting on the 27th July, when Mr. Bancroft produced a plan of his proposed drainage scheme to abste the nuisance caused by sewage from Newtown, Cobden-st., ke., and sub- mitted an estimate of the cost, amounting to £673 11 s 2d, Including £6l 4s 81 for contingencies, if the sewage was passed on to the land, but exclusive of any expense ie forming the carriers, &e., the cost would be £346 16s. The above estimates were exclusive of land and wayleaves. After some consideration the Committee unanimously re- solved that the Authority be recommended to adopt Mr. Bancroft's scheme for conveying the sewage from Cobden- -8441, Newtown, etc., direct to the river at an estimated cost of £673 us 2d, exclusive of wayleaves, and that the soli- citor to the Authority be instructed to serve the necessary notices for wayleaves required, and prepare provisional egreements for such wayleaves.—Mr. Ashton, the chairman, not being present, Mr. WALLINGTON moved, and Mr. DARRY- saint seconded the adoption of the report.—Carried.

div.head: FEVER AT WESTON.
div.p: FEVER AT WESTON.

The MEDICAL OFFICER (Mr. J. G. Mcßryde) reported that one death from typhoid fever had been notified to him since the last meeting of the Sanitary Authority. John William Fletcher, of Green Gate, Alvanley, died from memingitis, coming on as a secondary affection or segnel of typhoid fever after an illness of eight days. The drinking water should be submitted to the analyst for his certificate. The number of cases of scarlet fever inspected by him during his visit to Weston and Weston Point was 13. With reference to Dr. George Buchanan's memorandum, as to the treatment or disposal of rags from Egypt, he thought it very improbable that such consignments would reach the Port of Runcorn. If, however, any should arrive he had requested to be sent for immediately.—This concluded the business.

ST. BEDE'S YOUNG MEN'S SOCIETY. APPLETON. The members of this society celebtrated the first anniver- sary of their existence on Saturday evening, when about 100 persons partook of an excellent supper in St. Bede's school- room. The following ladies presided at the tables :—Mrs. Edward Swift, Mrs. John Swift, Mrs. T. Dennett, Mrs. Cald- well, Mrs. Fitzpatrice, Mrs. W.D ennett, Miss Wright, Miss Forster, and Miss Brown. After the repast, the assembly adjourned to another room, where a meeting and entertain- nient was held. The audience was largely increased. Mr. J. Morrison, the president Of the society, presided, and be was supported by the Rev. Father Finegan (chaplain to the society), Mr. Hirst (vice-president). Mr. Cowley. cud Mr. Hunt (the hon. secretary). In a few appropriate sentences, the CfrAutzwer proposed a vote of thanks to the ladies for the gracious and kindly way in which they had assisted the members of the society at supper.—Mr. COWLEY seconded the motion, which was heartily carried • and the Rev. Father FINEGAN responded in a genial speech. Mr. HUNT then read the annual report as follows : "The council in submitting this their first aenual report have to congratulate the members on the successor the society, since Its formation, on 20th August. 1882.. Uhere are nsw over 80 reliable members, and the attendance at the weekly meet- ings is exceedingly satisfactory. At the vc,:oskty meetings of members pape-s have been read by the Rev. Father Finegan (chap!ain), Messrs. Morrison (oresident), Cowley, Themas, Joseph, Austin. William Hunt, William Leatherharrow, John Dennett, Conroy, and Quinn. During the winter three public lectures were given under the auspices of the society; one by our rev chaplain, Father Finegan, subject, • Young Men's Soeieties. their objects and adv tntages ; ' one by the Rev Father Gallagher, entitled, • Inurdes and its Memories ; ' and the other by the Rev. Father Barker, on the Human Soul;' and the c emelt take this opportunity of record:ng the thanks of the members to the gentlemen named for their kindness in giving their able services to the society. The proceeds of the first two lectures, realis;ng 211 15s 6tl wag div:ded ; heti being given to the funds of the society, and the other half to the "New e'chool" fund. The whole of the proceeds of ti-e third lecture wee given to the New Sch.ol fund. A library Ism been formed, and there are novr upwards of 60 books in the society's posses- sloe. Boilcs and papers have been given by Mr. Deacon. Mr Bradshaw. and Mr. Frank Reyes, and th 3 thanks of the so ciety are due to these kind doners for their handsome presents. As regard, finance, our total income amounts to £32 I7s 44. and our eitpenditureoncluding £5 for us of schoolroorn,amount4 to £25 lie Id, leaving a balance in the treasurer's hands of £7 Is 31. At the end of the year there will be £5 due for hire of the pia,a 1. but as the society have the option of purchase,t he council hope the members will, in some way, rai,e the neces- sary ameunt to make the instrument the properly of the so ciety. In closing this report, the eau:tell, on behaif of the members, tender to the rev, chaplain tlx-ir very earnest, thanks. for establishing in the parish this orga.ni-atien, and for the zealous manner in which he has, at all. times, laboured'for the society since its formation." The CHAIRMAN, in the course of moving the adoption of the report, said : It is not the members only that a society of this kind benefits, but it influences for good the whole of the parish, and I think I may venture to assert that ' the society has already made *its mark. I am sure there is more earnestness in the congregation and a stronger disposition to support every good work than there was before this society existed. Yen all know with what facility we raised the necessary funds to complete the organ, and I put this down to the existence of this society. When I made the proposition to our rev, chaplain that we should complete the organ, which meant an expenditure of about £l5O, I said that with the supp3rt and assistance of the Young Men's Society we could easily raise the money, he replied, " I quite agree with you, and you may put me down for £5 to start with." (Applause.) Two members of the Young Men's Society collected the money, the -organ has been completed, the wetk paid for, and we have now an instrument in the beautiful church in which it is our happiness to worship. (Applau.e.) I have been exceedingly pleased with the spirit of forbearance which appeared to animate the members in all their busi- ness proceedings during the past 12 months. Very often societies of this kind fail through petty jealousies, some members retiring because they disagree with the majority, bat, we have had nothing of this kind, and I hope we never shall. (Applause.) I trust we shall always be guided by the precepts expressed so beauitifully in the prayer with which we open our weekly meetings, viz., "Prudence in our councils, humility in our thoughts, charity in our word?, and a mutually loving, forbearing, and fraternal spirit." Depend upon it that if we are actuated by such motives, we are safe to succeed. We have begun well, and I hope and trust we shall continue to work amicably together, perse- vering in every good work, and rendering to our pastor that support which he needs in the. many responsibilities con- nected with the working of this important mission. (Ap- pleuse.) Mr. Hirst seconded the adoption of the report. The Rev. Father Finegan supported the resolution, and in doing so asserted that the society bad done a great work. That it had been a blessing to the congregation and dietriet he had no hesitation in saying. (Hear, hear.) The external advantages offered by the society in mutual intercourse, social meetings, and a library, though very valuable, were small, compared with the spiritual advantages which the members had received during the past year. He had no hesitation in saying that he was proud to be the chaplain of such a society, and, he hoped the conduct which had marked their existence during the past twelve months, would he theirs in the future; that never would it be his disagreeable lot to rebuke or chastise them publicly; that when they- went through the streets, they would go as worthy members of the society, firm as the adainantine rock in the faith which was theirs, and of which they as Catholics knew the value, (hear, hear), at the same time giving offence to none, because it was the true spirit of Catholicity, and Christianity that whilst they were ready to die for their faith, they were ready to xtend the hand of charity to their fellow-citizens who disagreed With them on the principles of religion. (Applause.) He wenld !intim, he said, the idea of being chapl,in to any society that was not able to conduct themselves. in a Christianlike and becoming manner; and he exhorted them to adhere to their faith, to be just in their dealings with their neighbours, and charitable to everyone with whom they came in contact. (Applause.) Mr. COWLEY, whom the chairman introduced as a descen- dent of a family whose name had been associated with Catholicity in that the resolution is an appropriate speech. parish for many generaeions, supported The musical programme was then commenced by the piano- fiSrte solo "My Queen" played with much skill by Mr. John Caldwell; Mr. Lewton, a vocalist of greet merit, sang "Every bullet :bee its billet," in a style which drew fot th a hearty encore from the atielience, anti he kindly responded

ON SATURDAY NExr, AUG-LIST 18ru, Will appear in The Examiners the Opening Chapters of A NEW TALE EIiTITLRD„ Too IIIbOBBING 'PETER TO PAY PAUL," By JOHN SAUNDRA& The Story is one of the best from the pen of this gifted newspaper novelist, and will be found to be deeply interesting. Though be- longing to a healthy awe of fiction, it is vet free rom any thing approaching So esermonizing. The merits of the author wilt be best attested by the following opinion of a previous novel, "Love's Martyrdom," from the pen of the late Charles Dickens : " I can say that I read it with the closest attention, and that it inspired me with a strong interest, and a genuine and high ad- miration. The parts that involved some of the greatest difficulties of your task appear to me those in which you shine most. I would particularly instance the end of Julia as a very striking example of this. The delicacy and beauty of her redemption from her weak, rash lover are very far Indeed beyond the range of any ordinary dramatist, and display the true poetical strength."

div.head: Zetteto to the editor.
div.p: Zetteto to the editor.

OUR NATIONAL CHURCH. SIR,—I hasten to correct an error in mv letter under this heading in Saturday's Examiner. I stated that the Primate in his recent speech at the meeting of the Church Defence Institution said that in one diocese 39 churches and some odd missions had been omitted from the returns of the recent religious census. The letter was written away from home, and I had not the speech by me at the time to refer to, so that I had to rely on my memory. I find now, on looking at the speech, that it was in one town where 17 churches and six mission chapel., served by 39 clergymen, were emitted from Mr. Fowler's returns. The number of clergy (39) will to some extent explain how I should have fixed on 39 churches.—Yours, H. J. WESTBROOK. SlR,—Under this beading a letter appeared in your issue of Saturday last, written by Mr. H. J. Westbrook, in which he stated he knew some little episodes connected with the circuit dinners of a certain dissenting body. Now, as he challenges "Clifford Dix" to substantiate his statement with regard to the attendance at Trinity Church, will he be so good as to substantiate his own with reference to the above circuit dinners? for, as he says, "these are statements which are easy to make, but most difficult to prove," and why he should have attacked the Dissenting bodies at all is past my comprehension.—l am, sir, Warrington, August, 1883. AN OBSERVER. Sir,—Your correspondent" H. J. Westbrook," need not be as sensitive regarding the attendance at Holy Trinity 'Church. Not long ago I visited this edifice, during service, and as on opening the door I could see no one, I concluded the congregation were buried in the old-fashioned pews at prayer. But hearing voices, I proceeded a little further, and then to my surprise discovered the congregation was composed of two persons—the curate, who was reading the prayers, and the vicar's wife, who responded. So much for" H. J. Westbrook's" challenge respecting Holy Trinity Church.—Yours, dm. VISITOR. Warrington, August, 1883.

div.head: L A.TE PLOWER AND FRUIT SHOW AT LYM M.
div.p: THE L A.TE PLOWER AND FRUIT SHOW AT LYM M.

Sir,—! was very pleated te see from your report of this show that everything passed off satisfactorily, and that the show was a success. I understand an effort is to be made to continue the show upon a much larger scale another year. Might I be permitted to suggest to the committee, or those in authority, that as it is essentially a " cottagers' " show, steps may be taken which will ensure that any person shall not be allowed to exhibit anything unless satisfactory proof be pro- duced that it is the exhibitor's own productital. Ugly rumour has it that several exhibitors obtained prizes for vegetables, dm, which could not possibly have been grown by the exbibitors themselves; and as this is widely rumoured throughout the district, unless some such satisfactory pro- vision be made, and an assurance given by the committee, no doubt many people will decline to compete at the next show. Legally there is no doubt that if any persons has.os obtained prizes for produce exhibited by them, and profess- ing to have been growa upon their own ground, when in reality they were either borrowed or bought for the occa- sion, are liable to prosecution for obtaining money by false pretences. If this letter should catch the eyo of any such person, no doubt upon reflection he will see his way to return the amount of his prizes to the comMittee of the show as a kind of "conscience money," or silould this course be objectionable, he could (anonymously of , course) remit the amount to the Infirmary of this town. ON THE LOOK OUT. Warrington, August 9th, 1883.
THE RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE BEA.SLEY BILLS. •

Our attention has been called to your report of the speech of Dr. McDougall at a meeting of the Runcorn Improve- ment Commissioners held on Wednesday last, in which he quotes certain items from our bill of costs in the action of Beasley v. the Runcorn Commissioners. With oneexception all the items in question simply prove this: that many of the Commissioners (to their honour be it said) disclaimed having taken any part in the unjustifiable proceedings against Mr. Beasley, and some had even strongly opposed such proceedings. These Commissioners need no defence from us, as any fair-minded person will readily perceive that under such circumstances they took the proper and only consistent course in informing us, as Mr. Beasley's solicitors, of their disapproval of and opposition to the illegal pro- ceedings referred to. We did not wish to go on with the action against gentlemen who had taken no part in these proceedings against Mr. Beasley, although we were obliged to serve writs upon all the Commissioners in consequence of the Law Clerk refusing to allow us to inspect the minutes of the meetings when the aforesaid proceedings were resolved upon. The Law Clerk did send us a garbled extract from the minutes of some of the meetings in question, but it will scarcely be believed when we say that this extract actually suppressed the names of the Commissioners present ! The following (omitting formal parts only) is a copy of the letter from our firm, which accompanied the writ, and it speaks for itself:— "Inspection of the Commissioners' minute books, or a complete extract therefrom, with the object of ascertaining which of the Commissioners authorised the proceedings in respect of which this action is brought, having been persis- tently denied to us by.their clerk and solicitor, who also re- fuses to accept service on your behalf, no option is left us but to serve the writ separately upon each of the members. Our process-server, therefore, waits upon you with a copy of the writ which it is requisite we should hand to you Personally. The plaintiff will be entitled to inspection of the minute books at a later stage of the action, and if it be then found that you did not assist in passing or confirming the resolutions complained of, or did not sanction the steps which were afterwards taken professedly in pursuance of them, the action so far as you are concerned will be discontinued, or If we receive your assurance that you in no way participated or concurred in what was done, you need not enter appearance?, It was in reply to this letter that many of the Commission- ers made the communications to us which have aroused the anger of Dr. MacDougall, who, we suppose, would have had these innocent Commissioners cast in their lot with those who instigated or approved of the proceedings against Mr. Beasley. We have only one other explanation to make, and that is with regard to the item dated July 20, 1882, and which is incorrectly quoted by Dr. MacDougall. It reads thus in the bill: "July 20. Attending Mr. Speakman when he made important statements to us affecting the liability of the Commissioners." [There is no charge made for this in the bill, the item being scored up.] The nest item reads : "Drawing further observations for counsel, including Mr. Tremblett's proof for 19 [at is], 195." The statements referred to are easily explained, and here again it will be seen that Dr. MacDougall has bit upon a veritable "mare's nest." A few days before the trial five of the Commissioners, viz., Dr. Steele, Mr. Norman, Mr. Hazle- ' burst, Mr. Briscoe, and Mr. J. J. Speakman, committed a contempt of court in not filing answers to the plaintiff's interrogatories pursuant to an order of the court. We accordingly took out a summons to enforce the order, and it then transpired from the Law Clerk's admissions that these five Commissioners could not be got to answei the in4rrogatories. It was thus evident (and indeed it had been from the very first) that the

essore.---- Runcorn Commissioners could only be cempared to " a, house divided against itself." Two days before the trial, whilst waiting for the case to come on, we casually met Dr. 'Reale and Mr. Speakman in the Assize Courts, Manchester, eged in the course of a short conversation we asked them tow it was that the five Commissioners were still defending the action, andlet would not answer the plaintiff's inter- rogatories. To this they replied that these Commissioners could not adopt the answers to interrogatories sworn by the other Commissioners, and were not going to incur any per- sonal liability or prejudice their position (as they thought) by swearing any affidavits in the action. These are the im- portant statements (but they were opinions rather than state- ments) referred to In our bill of costs, and no ether state- ments were made. Of course it must have been well known to the Commissioners' counsel, Mr. Gully, that a number of the Commissioners were in contempt for not answering the plaintiff's interrogatories, and he would doubtless draw his own conclusions as to the significance of such a defection in the ranks of the defendants. The "further observations to connel" composing the other item in the bill of which Dr. McDougall made so much had nothing whatever to do with any statements made by Mr. Speakman or Dr. Steele, and we shall be happy to pro- duce these further observations to Dr. McDougall so that he may satisfy himself upon that score. This fact alone is conclusive to show that Dr. McDougall is altogether wrong in the construct'on he puts upon the item in question, for if statements of the nature he insinuates had really been made to us they would, without doubt, have appeared in these "Further observations." We think the ratepayers of Runcorn ought to know that on the 4th July, 1892, two days before the search warrant was issued against Mr. Beasley, he wrote to the commis- sioners informing them that, with one exception, the paltry articles alleged to have been feloniously stolen were actually his own property, and as to the excep- tfon—a pair of poles worth about 2s 6i—the man who had removed them, entirely by mistake, had been directed to replace them. And yet with this letter staring them in the face, and without even calling upon Mr. Beasley for an explanation some of the Commissioners and their legal adviser proceeded to to get a sworn information laid and a search warrant issued. If these persons still con- sidered they had a good defence to Mr. Beasley's action, they cannot be congratulated on their knowledge of the law. Their own counsel. Mr. Gully, Q.C., on the trial said that he" had ativised and strong advised the Commissioners that they had no defence "to the action. The fact of the Commissioners being a "divided body " was known to their legal advisers at the least six months before the trial, and therefore could not have been the sole reason for consenting to a judgment, for had the Commis- sioners been ever so united it would have been impossible for them to justify their proceedings in a court of law in the face of Mr. Beasley's letter of the 4th July, 1882. A printed copy of the shorthand notes of the trial will now be printed and circulated amongst the ratepayers by our client, and, if necessary, a copy of the answers to inter- rogatories sworn by some of the Commissioners. JONES di PRIDE. 26, North John-street, Liverpool, 9th Aug., 1883.

THE LATE RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT EARLESTOWN. Sir,—At the ratepayers' meeting held on the 25th ultimo, I, in criticising the report issued by the Commissioners for the year ending March 25th, 1883, stated that the Commis- sions had transferred £l,OOO from the gas and water ac- counts to the general improvement account during the last three years. Mr. Fakelough being a Commissioner at the time, asserted that I also was a Commissioner at the time. I replied that it was seven years since I was a Commissioner, consequently I could not be present at the time the transfers were made. Mr. Fairclough afterwards re-asserted what he had previously stated, and called the reporters attention to it in order to make it appear that I had been a consenting party to the transaction, which I deny. The last year I sat as a member of 'the Board of Commissioners was in 1875, and the transfers to which I object took place—the first for £6OO in 1881, the second for £2OO in 1882, and the third for £2OO in 1883 ; so that it was impossible for me to have been a consenting party to the transaction. So much for Mr. Fairclough's assertion, to which he called the reporters particular attention.—' am, yours, dm., GEORGE APPLETON.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.-SATURDAY.

MISCELLANEOUS.—After a little "scene" caused by Mr. A.shmead-Bartlett, the second readings 3f the Voters' Regis- tration (Ireland) Bill and the Union Officers' Superannua- tion (Ireland) Bill were carried on division; the Local Government (Scotland) Bill passed the same stage; and the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Bill and the Patents Bill were read a third time. Progress having been made with the Irish Labourers Bill, the Payment of Wages in Public Houses Prohibition Bill, and the Pigeon Shooting Bill, the House adjourned at a quarter to eight, having sat since shortly after noon. HOUSE OF LORDS.—MONDAY.

The Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Bill was read a first time.—Lord STRATIIEDEN and CAMPBELL moved for copies of the original concessions to M. de Lesseps with regard to the Isthmus of Suez. His lordship's critcisms, and those of the Marquis of Salisbury, of the policy of the Go- vernment in the matter were met by an offer by Earl Gran- ville of an opportunity to raise a debate on the subject. In the end the motion was withdrawn.—Several measures were advanced a stage, including the Railway Passenger Duty, Szc., Bill, which passed its second reading. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. _
