HOUSE OF LORDS-THURSDAY.

The Earl of CAMPERDOWN reported from the committee on the Manchester Ship Canal that in their opinion it was not expedient to proceed further with the bill.—The Patents Bill was read a second time, and the Railway Passenger Duty Bill a third time, after Lord Brabourne had ineffectu- ally moved the omission of a clause which gives the Board of Trade power to interfere with railway companies not providing sufficient accommodation for third class pas- sengers at one penny per mile fare.—Upon the motion to read a second time the Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Bill, the Duke of ARGYLL complained that, while it was de- clared by Lord Carlingford to be identical with the English bill, the provision that the tenant should not receive com- pensation for improvements actually flowing from the soil had been omitted from the Scotch bill. His grace announced that in committee he should move amendments, and if these were accepted,he would vote for the bill,though " he did not see its necessity for Scotland."—The Duke of RICHMOND and li-orenole, on the contrary, supported the bill in the threefold interests of landlord and incoming and outgeing tenants.—The bill was read a secoad time.—lt was explained by the Earl of Krinnent,Ev, in answer to a question, that no treaty or commercial engagement had been entered into with the Ameer of Afghanistan, but that the annual subsidy was an aid to the military and other expenses of defending his territory.

EXTRAORDINARY TITHES. Replying to Mr. Daniel Grant, the HOME SECRETARY hoped the question of extra- ordinary tithes might bo settled next session. LUNATIC PAUPER CHILDREN. Mr. MUNDELLA, in a statement about the apparent increase in the number of lunatic pauper children, said that nine-tenths of the idiocy among such children is due to parental intemperance, a fact which should not escape the attention of social reformers. div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

WINSFORD ANNIVERSARIES —The annual sermons were preached on Sunday at the Station Road Primitive Metho- dist Chapel, by the late superintendent of the circuit, the Rev. W. Forth, of Burton-on-Trent. The rev, gentleman gave a lecture on "Bunyan " on Monday, when Mr. John Stubbs occupied the chair. The proceeds of both days were about £l7.—On Sunday, Mr. S. Bailey, of Crewe, preached the anniversary sermons in connection with the United Free Methodist Mission Room, Delamere-street. On Monday, Mr. Sadler; of Moulton, delivered a special address on "The Resurrection," when the chair was taken by the Mayor of Over (Mr. Jovph Slater). The Sunday school children in connection with these places of worship, had treats consisting of tea, cake, drc. On Friday afternoon the Primitive scholars had a regular field day, enjoying their sports in the open air, in a rield adjoining, up to 9 p.m. The Wesleyan Sunday School (Hill Top) had their annual sport day and feast at Mr. Latham's Clive. It happened, unfortunately, to rain hard at intervals during the day, which greatly damped the ardour of the little folks, though it had not the effect of keeping them away from follow- ing their new drum and fife band at its first public appear- anee.

THE DYNAMITE CONSPIRACY. H°P TRIAL OF THE SE'. HELENS AND LIVERPOOL 111, OP PRISONERS. At the Liverpool Assitee, ori Tiiestiay, before Mr. Justice Stephen, Timothy Featherstone, 30, described as a school- master; Daniel O'Herlihy, 36, stationer ; Denis Leasey, 31, railway porter • Patrick Flanagan, 27, railway brakeman; and Henry Dalton, alias John Henry O'Connor, 39, printer, were brought up on charges of being in possession of illegal explosives, with intent to commit a felony, conspiring to blow up public and other buildings, conspiracy to murder , subjects of Her Majesty, and treason felony. Special arrangements had been made regarding the admission of visitors to the court, and every precaution taken to prevent any demonstration or ebullition of feeling on the part of friends of the prisoners. Sir Fairer Herschell, Q.C., M.P. (solicitor-General), Mr. J. B. Aspinall, Q.C., and Mr. R. S. Wright conducted the case for the Crown ; Mr. Addison, Q C., Dr. Commins, M.P., and the Hon. A. D. Elliott was retained on Featherstone's behalf; Mr. McConnell appeared for O'Her- lihy; Dr. O'Feeley represented Flanagan and Deasey ; and Mr. Little defended Dalton. The prisoners each pleaded "Not guilty."—The empanelling of the jury was then pro- ceeded with, each juror being sworn as he entered the box, and every facility afforded to the prisoners to challenge or object to them.—The Solicitor-General opened the case for the prosecution. He explained that the acts charged against the prisoners were the same, the purpose and object only being indifferently stated; and having given a general out- line of the character of the evidence to be adduced, con- cluch d by remarking that it was very important to the public that offences of this nature—so wide-spread and so terrible in their results—should, if proved, be severely pun- ished.—Evidence was then called as to the arrival of Featherstone in Liverpool by the steamer Indiana, and as to the purchase by him of carboys of nitric and sulphuric acids in Glasgow, and their 'ming sent to Cork, where they were received by O'Herlihy and Deasey. Evidence as to Deasey's arrival on the Liverpool Landing- stage having then been given, Detective-Superintendent " Williams' of the Liverpool police, deposed to examining Deasey's box the night he was arrested, and to finding two tin canisters containing lignine dynamite, a parcel labelled chlorate of potash, one labelled powdered sugar, and another containing realgar or red orpiment. Three brass taps were • also found. The contents were handed over to Dr. Camp- bell Brown, the city analyst, for examination On the 6th of July he was informed that the prisoner Flanagan wished to see him, and Captain Nott Bower, the head constable, accompanied him to the gaol. Flanagan asked him if he had found a letter which Featherstone had written to him (Flanagan), and be went on to ask the question whether witness was aware that Featherstone only came back from America a little before last Christmas, and stayed and slept with him at St. Helens, on the 30th and 31st of December. Prisoner then Said "When you took Deasey, how was it you came to make the mistake of 34 insteadof 43, Regent-street. becaused that is how you missed the other man." Prisoner did not say who the other man was. He then made some allusion to Dr. Campbell Brown's examination, and endeavoured to explain that Dr. Brown was wrong as to the mixture of the materials to form dynamite. Prisoner also said that he belonged to the Fenian organization, and that he joined it in et. Helens some two years ago. Flanagan further made the remark "You know I don't wish to turn informer. Of course they can't give us what they gave those people in London, because they dealt with them under the new Act." —Cross-examined by Dr. O'Feeley: This was the first time this conversation had been mentioned in open court, but it had been transmitted to the Treasury. Dr. O'Feeley com- plained that he had not been furnished with a copy of this evidence.—Cross-examination continued: He did not say anything about Norman or the other London prisoners to Flanagan, but a question might have been asked by the prisoner concerning them. The prisoner put several ques- tions to him, and he had not told prisoner that he would get penal servitude for life.—Robert Fitzwilliam Starkie, a sub-inspector of theßoyal Irish Constabulary stationed atCork, stated that on the 29th of March last he arrested the prisoner Featberstcne at a refreshment-house in Warren's-place, Cork. A constable named Walsh searched the prisoner in the pre- sence of witness, and there was found on him a green docu- ment purporting to be a cure for gout (but which was really a direction for making a combustible compound), a letter, dated the 20th March, addressed to Messrs. J. Montgomerie and Co., Glasgow, °uterine four carboys of nitric acid, and an old envefope addressed to O'Herlihy, and bearing the Glasgow postmark. The room was searched by Constables Vaughan and Walsh, and a glass tube with a cork in it, known as a test tube, was found in a black bag, an several cards of membership of religious cenfraternities in America, be iring the name of Edward 0.8. Kennedy.—Cross-examined by Dr. Cummins : He had seen the prisoner Deasy in Walton Gaol since his committal without having been sent for, and wit hout.any one else being present. His object in seeing him was to obtain what information he could.—Cross- examined by Dr. O'Feeley: He had seen Flanagan in Walton I Gaol in the presence of Featherstone, and had asked him if Featheistone was the man he had alluded to in a statement to another official, and Flanagan said "No." O'Herlihy was then brought in, and Flanagan having been asked the same question replied in the nega- tive. He did not rezellect speaking to Flanagan about the London or any other prisoeere, and he (id not say that the prisoner had better give information than get penal servi- tude for life.—Several officials from the Cork Post Office were then called to show that money orders purporting to be drawn by O'Herlihy had been issued for transmission to Glasgow, and that letters addressed to the proprietor at Great George-street West, were delivered at 77 Shandon-st.— , Archibald Barr was called to give evidence concerning the explosion at the Possilroad Bridge, Glasgow, on the 21st inst.—After the examination of some other witnesses, the Coart adjeurned. The trial was resumed on Wednesday.—lnspector Little- child, of the Metropolitan Police, deposed to the arrest of Dalton at Dowles' American Reading-room in the Strand. II a amcket-book fouad upon him were several entries re- lating to the msrmfacture of fulminate of silver, fulminate of mercury, and other chemicals; and in his house at Eden- place several letters were found, and also a glass tube and other things.—James Enwriebt, a constable of the Metro- politan Police Force, spoked to having watched Dalton And a companion on the 24th March, looking at Westminster Abbey and the Houses of Parliament, and making notes in a book.—William Lammie, a tailor, said that in 1867 he was sworn into the Fenian Brotherhood. In the year 1868 he left Dublin, and returned in 1878. Some time afterwards be attended Fenian meetings frequently. The meetings were held twice a week, and from 50 to 80 persons attended, according to accommodation. Drill was carried on, and collections made for arms and civil purposes. In the organisation the centres were the heads, the B's under the centres, and the C's under the B's.—Colonel Majendie, R.A., Her Majesty's Chief Inspector of Explosives, deposed to receiving from the Procurator Fiscal at Glasgow a tin box containing some material like sawdust, and a brass tap, which he handed to Dr. Dupre. The matesial was lignine dynamite, and was similar to some found at the T;2c eflice and some brought from Liverpool found in Deasey's box. It was not an ex- plosive licensed for manufacture or importation in this country.—James Campbell Brown, professor of chemistry at the University College, Liverpool, said each canister con- tained about cwt. of material which was composed of saw- dust and nitro-glycerine. There was an average of 75 per cent. of nitro-glycerine, 23 per cant. of sawdust, and 2 per cent. of chalk.—The case for the prosecution having closed, counsel for the defence urged that there was no case to go to the jury.—Mr. Justice Steethen agreed that the case against O'llerlihy was weak, and the Solicitor-General said after that expression of opinion he would not proceed any fur- tlpr against the prisoner.—A form ti verdict of not guilty was returned, and O'Herlihy left the dock, but was informed by his Lerdship that he might be indicted on a minor count. his Lordship felled that the case against the other prisoners must go to the jury, and the Court adjourned. VERDICT AND SENTENCE. The trial was brought to a close on Thursday. The counsel for the defence contended that there was no evidence of con- spiracy between the accused, nor that they were parties to a larger conspiracy to levy war upon the Government by acts which might result in damage to property and injury to persons or loss of life inflicted upoe him:cant people. As to the possession of explosives, it was argued that the dynamite might have been used for the purpose of taking fish, or to support a colliers' strike, or for a commercial pur- pose." Sulphuric acid such as was found upon Flanagan was, the jury were told, used medicinally, especially by per- sons engaged in heavy toil. The description of Fenian fire_ was, counsel suggested, what a newspaper correspondent would naturally desire to send in one of his letters to America, where the Irish movement had created so much interest.— The Solicitor-General, in reply, said the jury had heard a good deal of powerful declamation, and many ingenious suggestions, but had waited he vain for any explanation of the facts which told so seriously against the prisoners.—His Lordship, in a charge which occupied two hours, summed up with great weight and impressiveness, remarking" that the strength of the contry consisted in its justice, and that its justice consisted in daring to do right under all circum- stances and in the face of all and every kind of prejudice which might influence the judgment."—The jury, after an absence af fifty-five minutes, returned into court with a ver- dict of guilty against all four prisoners.—Only two of the accused, Dalton and Flanigan replied to the customary in- terrogation, and they simply denied the charge of conspiracy, but offered no shadow of explanation for the circumstances which led to their trial.—His lordship briefly sentenced the prisoners to penal servitude for life, and they were shortly afterwards removed to Walton Gaol. ANOTHER ARREST. At Liverpool, on Tuesday, James M'Dermott was re- manded charged with conspiracy to murder public officials in Treland and at Liverpool. Prisoner was apprehended on board a steamer on arrival from America. He had travelled, it was alleged, under an assumed name, and correspondenoe with O'Donovan Rossa and James Stephens was found upon him.

div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF A %O MAN AT ST. HELENS. - On Tuesday afternoon Mr. T. W. Barker held an inquest at the Feathers Inn, Westfield-street, St. Helens, on the body of Mary Filiinghani. aged 42 years, wife of William Filling- ham, collier, of 16, Eccleston—street, who died shortly after confinement on Saturday evening, having been attended by a midwife. As a sudden change took place a medical gentleman was sent for, but she expired shortly after his arrival. He declined to give a certificate, stating as his reason that had medical assistance been obtained earlier the life -of the woman might have been saved.—The Coroner went fully and carefully into all the evidence, which satisfied the jury, and they returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes."

THE FLOWER SHOW AT altlIf• This show, which on the whole has been a success closed on Saturday evening, when the prizes (a list of which has ' already appeared in these columns) were distributed to the winners by Mrs. Guest, wife of the rector of Lynam. Pre- vious to the distribution, the Rector (the Rev. G. W. Guest, M.A.) addressed a few words to the exhibitors and visitors. He said Our show has been on the whole a very successful one, and we may fairly congratulate ourselves. We have been favoured with splendid weather, and through the kindness of Mr. Battersby we have had one of the prettiest sites pos- sible for our tents. There has been much to be admired in every department. In the art work tent there are some beautiful specimens of handiwork, and in plants and flowers the delay is most creditable ; whilst the bee exhibition, managed by Mr. Parker, of Altrineham (an enthusiastic and successful member of the Cheshire Bee- keepers Association), is most excellent- and instructive. I, at any rate, have learned more about the habits and management of bees than I have ever known before. But successful though our show is, mach more might have been done if we could have managed to drive into our neighbours heads that there was to be an exhibition, and that it was worth their while to compete. A gentleman who has known this neighbourhood for some years told me yesterday that it took twelve months to drive anything into the heads of the people in this part of the world, and I begin to think he is right; for we have been nearly twelve months hammering away, and some have only just begun to realise that a flower show and exhibition is contemplated. Indeed, I don't know whether some have yet realised it, though they have seen the tents; for if they had I think they would have spared a shilling to give themselves the pleasure of a walk round the show ground. We have been told that a flower show opens the door to dishonesty. What is there, I should like to ask, in this world of ours that does not? We hear now and then of an unscrupulous farmer using water for another purpose than washing out his milk cans; can it be said that we who like a little cream in our tea or coffee are opening the door dishonestly by buying milk? Think what exhi- bitions of various kinds have crone for this country. What would have ben the condition of some of our manufac- tures probably now had not a stimulus to improvement been I given by the great exhibition of 1851? Then, again, what wonderous improvements have been brought about in every- thing connected with agriculture and horticulture, entirely , in consequence of the encouragement given by exhibitions. But these are by no means all the advantages of exhibi- tions. They give people something to think about, their , minds become enlarged, their tastes more refined, and they learn to realise more and more the blessings of indus- try. Now, Whatever drawbacks we have had to con- tend with let us not be cast down by them, but begin to look ferward to a grande'r show next year. No time must be lost. Your onions and cabbage for 1884 must be put in before long, begin to think about the best kinds now. Your geranium cuttings should soon be in, begin to look out for the best sorts. The short days will soon be upon us, begin to think what you can employ yourselves in on the long evenings for exhibition next year. And new let me offer the thanks of the committee to all who have in any way helped to make this exhibition the success it has been ; and first of all to the ladies who have so kindly in- terested themselves, particularly Miss Morland Crosfield,Mrs. Morris, Mrs. Thomas, Mrs. Ernest Crtsfield ; the Misses Battersby, who have so kindly and so successfully presided at the fruit and refreshment tent; also Mr. Bat- tersby, for his kindness in allowing us the use of his beau- tiful park; to the judges for the careful and conscientious way in which they did their work; to the gardeners of the neighbourhood, particularly to Messrs. Bennett, Clark, Simpson, Taylor, and Hughes, who have done so much to make the show successful • to Mr. Parker, for his splendid collection of byes and bee-keeping appliances; to Mr. Abel Ellison, for exhibiting the process of fustian cutting; to Mr. Wickers, of the Fleece Hotel, for the excellent way in which he managed the refreshment department; and to our worthy secretary, Mr. Joseph Smith, who has worked, I may say, almost night and day to stir up an interest in the show, and to organise and carry out what was necessary to bring it to its present state of perfection.—The prizes were then presented by Mrs. Guest, and thus ended most success- fully the flower show of 1883.

further discussion was adjourned till Thursday. In the meantime Mr. Bicknell had been instructed to obtain a report from Mr. Leyland, veterinary surgeon, upon the horse, and that gentleman's report was now read, to the effect that it was a good harness mare, and would suit the purposes of the Board with proper driving. But he did not consider the old man employed competent to drive horses.—Mr. Birchall and Mr. Meadows having explained their respective shares in the transaction, the CHAIRMAN remarked that the subject was one upon which there should be no bickering. He pointed out that a majority of the committee had concurred in purchase of the horse.—On the *motion of Mr. HALL, it was left to the House Committee to consider whether the horse should be retained, or a contract entered into with some post master for the hire of horses and vehicles. THE CHARGE AGAINST A MEDICAL OFFICER. At last meeting letters were produced, but not read, con- taining charges against the medical officer for Sutton, of neglecting pauper patients. The letters were referred to the General Purposes Committee, who reported that the charges were entirely without foundation.—Mr. HALL stated that had Dr. Casey come before the committee he would have been told that he was doing his work satisfactorily, and that there was no ground of complaint against him. The persons complained of as haying been neglected were not on the books of the Union, or in any way concerned with Dr. Casey.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday, present: Mr. Tyrer (chairman), Rev. T. Finegan, Messrs. Meadows, Hall, Leatherbarrow, Eatock, Buckley, Jackson, Birchall, P. Longton, Syder, Kenwright, Newsome, Marsh, Matthews, Gerrard, Fisher. and Hartley (clerk.) MASTER'S REPORT. The MASTER reported that there were in the Workhouse 424 inmates, as compared with 430 in the preceding week, and 442 in the corresponding week of last year. During the week 55 vagrants had been relieved. In July of last year the number relieved was 126. INCREASED SALARIES. Letters were read from the Local Government Board sanctioning the increases of salary recommended at a previous meting of th:r Board to Mr. Stuart, relieving officer; and Mr. and Mrs. Bicknell, master and matron of the Work- house.

WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. The fourth quarterly meeting of the Council was held at the Town Hell, on Tuesday. The Mayor (Councillor Cros- field) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Bur- gess, Davies, Chandley, Webster, Holmee, and Thewlis ; Councillors Monks, Wallington, W. Pierpoint, Mackie, Woollen, Greening, Barker, Broadbmt, Whittle, Litton, Dixon, Sutton, J. Fierpoint, and Elutchinson ; Mews. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Chorley (borough treaeuier), and T. Longdin (surveyor). Several ratepayers also attended. CITE CORPORATION AND THE BITER: AIT EXPLANATION. The MATOR said bJere moving the minutes of the Watch Committee he should like to occupy a minute or two of the Council's time with a statement regarding the river and the Corporation's control over D. The members would remem- ber that at the last Council meeting there was a long discus- sion about the ship canal and the river, and he noticed afterwards that tioencillor Dr. Mackie, in "The Guardian," referred to the time when the North-Western Railway Co. wiped to throw Ja the river at Fidler's Ferry— one 25 years ago, he thought it was---vgith the object of showing the paler of the Cctnoration over the river, jnas- much as the construction of the proposed bridge was pre- vented. He .wished te correct conncillca• Dr. Mackie on. that subject, beeause the construction of fie 'bridge was stopped by the evidence that was given by a captain in the employ of his firm; and he might add that if they had trusted to the Corporation the bridge would have been made and the navigation of the river would have been ruined. Counsel for the North-Western Railway told his (the Mayor's) brother afterwards that it was the evidence of their (Messrs. Crosfield's) captain that threw the bill out; and he thought he would just let the Council know that, as it showed the Corporation war very weak as regarded interfering with the river. Councillor Macau' asked to be allowed to say that the Mayor's statement that night was exactly the same as one he made at a public meeting three months ago, and some gentleman then present certainly claimed on behalf of the Town Council that it was the influential party. In fact, he presumed the evidence of no individual, connected even with a firm like Messrs. Crosfield's, could be said to have accomplished anything. He certainly had a good deal to do with the matter at the time, and be remembered very well that a gentleman at Runcorn now dead, who was the great mover In it, used to correspond with him almost weekly about it. He might say he had not the slightest hesitation in awarding all the credit due toliessrs.Crosfield's employes in the matter; at the same time he thought he must claim for the Corporation that jt did at that time as much as it was able to do, and that it certainly to some extent secured that the bridge should be made 75 feet clear of the water- way.

div.head: WIDENING OF BRIDGE-STREET.
div.p: THE WIDENING OF BRIDGE-STREET.

Councillor BROADBENt, in moving the adoption of the minutes of the Street Improvement and Lighting Commit- tee, observed that it would be noticed there was a recom- mendation for the widening of Bridge-etreet which he 'thought it would be better to discuss when the minutes of the General Purposes Committee came up for confirmar- Councillor BARBER seconded the motion. Alderman BURGESS asked if they were to pass the recom- mendation about the widening of Bridge-street as being of no importance, and go on to the General Purposes Commit- tee? fie thought they should discuss the matter then. The lgszoa: I think you are right, Alderman Burgess. I don't see why it should not be discussed now. Alderman DIEWLIS thought it would be the wisest course •to adopt. Alderman DAVIES drew attention to the fact that it was deeirable at that stage to discuse. the matter, because there was a recommendation to the General Purposes Committee, and the General Purposes Committee had a special resolution that the Council should be recommended to pass and adopt

it. Councillor BROADBENT said thiswas no new matter for the Council in one sense. It was thought, he supposed, by all members of the Council,that it was desirable to widen Bridge- and that so desirable an object could not be accomplished without funds was will known. In order to get the funds secured, part of theTbsoLation required that a Provisional Order be applied for. As they would be aware, he had been very much from home for sometime past, and his attendance at the committee meetings had not been so regular as it would be under ordinary circumstances. But he bad been in communication from time to time with the members of the committee and the Town Clerk on that subject, and he was entirely in ccord with the steps which had been taken. He believed they had been taken with the greatest possible judgment and sagacity, and that the purchases which had been so far made towards widening Bridge-street had been effected on terms as favourable as, or more favourable than, might have been hoped for. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS asked, without prejudicing his privi- lege of speaking later on, and he hoped without prejudice to the interests of the public, if they could be furnished with an idea as to what width it was proposed to widen that por- tion of Bridge-street they were widening, and at what cost it would ho done. He would also ask whether it was in the power of the committee to consider any further recom- mendation as to what length the widening of the street should go. Councillor BROADBEIbIT thought it had been decided to make the width of Bridge-street 40 feet. The I.llAvott said he thought the width of the street had to be about 45 feet. Councillor BROADBENT said quite recently when they had _ _ .
the pleasure ot his (the Mayor's) attendants at the com- mittee the matter was discussed, and the most desir,ible
width for Bridge-street was suggested, be thought, as 40 feet.
The MAYOR: 45 feet.

Councillor Broadbent remarked that there was a singular absence of Corporation officials just at that moment, but the Borough 'Surveyor would produce the plans and minute book. With regard to another part of the question he thought it had Wen found in the action of the committee that it was impossible to attempt to buy the whole strip on one side of the street and widen it right nif in that way. The best and only plan WAS that when they saw a piece of property that they could get easily to get it, and then wait their opportunity for -another piece, and so on, doing it by degrees. That had been the plan pursued in Bridge-street, and if they had taken any other plan they would have had to pay much more money for the property which had been acquired. The BOROUGH SURVEYOR produced the plans, and in reply to questions stated that the width of the street was to be 45 feet.
Alderman BURGESS : Can you give.- um any idea of the expenditure contemplated by that length?
Councillor BROADBENT : "i cannot. - The MAYOR: Probably it will not exceed £5,000.
Alderman BURGESS ; For 4.s_feet_?

The MAYOR: Tbat is the price that we anticipate for the land. It may not cost £l,OOO, bet at the outside I don't think it will cost more than £5,000. Alderman THRWLIS thought the Corporation would al- Wield be recouped by the re-sale of the property. The MAYOR: It is quite possible it may clear Alderman Timwtas thought it very probable. Councillor 13ROADBENT stated that so far they had been very fairly met by the owners of property. Alderman BURGESS asked if the cost of £5,000 included the re-formation of the street, paving, Jrc. The MAYOR: Oh, no. Alderman BURGESS: Nothing of the kind? The MAYOR: It is impossible to say what the cost will be until we know what we shall get back for the property. Alderman BURGESS said there would be no difficulty in knowing what the cost of reconstruction would be when they had got the width. The MAYOR thought they could get the cost of there- construction of the street easily enough. Councillor MACKIE thought they were not in a position to discuss such an important matter. They ought to be furnished with plans and specifications and particulars same as if they were directors of any company or if they were partners. He suggested that the discussion should be deferred for a month. They were all anxious that Bridge- street or any other narrow street in the town should be widened.

Alderman THEWLIS endorsed ouncillor Mackie's opinion that they should have full information as to the cost before they came to a definite decision. He was perfectly satisfied in bis own mind that they would recoup themselves, and it would be for the benefit of the town. He recollected when Market-street was altered there was a very large remunera- tion brought into the coffers of the Corporation, and eventually it was made by the profits arising from the gas works. Be thoroughly agreed with Dr. M'ackie that they should have more information upon the subject, which should be postponed, say for a month. Councillor BA.RIEET thought if the town clerk supplied them with the information given to the committee they would not require to postpone the mattcr for a month.

Alderman 1-31AvrE9 -observed that whatever statement the Town Clerk made would be within the hearing of the reports, and he thought it would I:te much better if the Tows Clerk 'were given a month to consider what should go forth to the public. (Hear, hear.) He made the suggestion in the interests ot the public and likewise of the Corpora- tion.

Alderman Bruones said he did not wish to throw any obstacle in the way of what was being done, but as they did not intend to get the Provisional Order until Parliament again met, he took it that nothing would be wrong if the Council considered the matter a month hence, so that the 41xcellent scheme might be a little more matured, if it required a little more maturing. There was one point he wished to mention for consideration, and that was the width they proposed to go to. They must bear in mind that it was propose.l to widen Bridge-street from Bridge-foot to Market-gate, and extend the street from thence right up to the uttermost end of the town. He thought it would be a judicious improvement if the mini- mum width of Bridge-street wag 60 feet or 20 yards. . They should go into other towns and see what was being done. They could not make a street for cottages less than 40 feet, and he did not think it would be a judicious sett'ement of the question to widen Bridge-street only to the extent of 45 feet.

The MAYOR said a suggestion had been made that the Council should have more information. He though t the the best plan would be as the town clerk recommended—to call a special meeting of the Town Council to sit in com- mittee and discuss the matter.

Alderman BURGESS suggested that the committee should reconsider the proposed width of the street, and that the borough surveyor furnish the committee with an estimate pf the cost of widening the street to 45 feet, and alto to 60
feet. If that were done they would find very little difference

in the cost. _7 The Tows- CLBRIC siid in dealing with matters of that \sort they could not ester into details without disadvantage to the public interests. He thought it would be advantae- ous to discuss the matter at a special meeting of the Coun. cil in committee, when every detail could be given them, such as was given to the committees. He would suggest . that the meeting be held on an early date. I C9Rhoillor 13sonh8,,NT said he would move the adoption I of the minuf a with the exception of the resolutions reftrring

to Bridge-street. Councillor BARKER seconded the motioti. Councillor MactitE asked if the committee had considered the question of widenng the street on the opposite side to that on which it was now proposed to widen it, in view of tho extension of the bridge which was to be made, he believed, in connection with the Ship Canal; also of tha2 street which was to bo made leading into Latchford' , for obtaining which he thought they were indebted to

Alderman Davies. The Mason. said he might tell them the committee did. consider the question of widening on the other side. ,f the street, and they had had councillor 6orinection with the canal? Tte MAYOR said he did not know about it beir.g la con- nection with the canal. That was the fir:A time he had heard the bridge was to be altered by the Canal Company. He thought it had to remain as it was. Councillor MACKIE thought they would revire a better bridge. The minutes were then passed. VISITORS TO TELE MUSEUM. Alderman WEBSTER move I that the minutes of the Museem. Library and Arts Committee be confirmed, and remarked that there was a decrease in the number of visitors to the various departments, but no doubt the attendance had ben influenced by the weather. He alluded to the report of Mr. Fell, who had attended tb,:, Fisheries Exhibition, and said he had no doubt that what the gentleman saw there would make itself manifest by a still further improvement in the casts of the fishes 'ne supplied to the institution. The rules had been printrei in the minutes for the purpose of meeting the requireakents of the Friendly Societies' Act, and with the view of berig sanctioned, to that they could see if they were entitled to to exempted lrom the rates. Councillor MA_cretz seconded tke motion, and explained 'at was necessary to insert the Tales in consequence of the Friendly Soo:ieties' Act. Aldermari Dsvins thouOt the report of the curator was not a very satisfactory one. The number of visitors for the month of June was 1,441, being a decrease of 8 per cent. from last year; the number of subscribers who had taken out books Yfas 2,105, a decrease of 2 per cent.; and the readers ntimlY4red 601, a decreare of 23 per cent. He thought that was v. very sad state of things—that the excellent oppor- tunities given to the people of Warrington were not more Vouncillor MACKIE: It is owing to the weather. Alderman DAVIES: You must bear in mind that this is a comparison with June, 1882. Councillor MACKIE: They have been wet Janes for seven years. Alderman DAVIES said he would be glad to see less im- providence amdngst the people. At any public institution in Warrington, he might say, the evidence of the improvi- dence was set forth. He did not think words spoken in that Council would be thrown away entirely if one asked the working people of Warrington to bear in mind that a day might come—and before long—when they would have to set their houses in order. as people had to do in hard times. When it was shown that men were not so careful as they were some 12 months ago, he did not think it was undesirable—he thought it was desirable and even warrantable—for them to make a few remarks of that kind. T.lO MAYOR quite agreed with Alderman Davies that nothing was more desirable tbaninculcating upon the work- ing classes the importance of being provident when they had the means. (Hear. hear) Improvidence was what the working classes were more guilty of than anything else, but he should be sorry indeed to think that the decrease in the number of visitors to the Museum was an indication of im- providence. He did not quite see it himself. He imagined it was owing more to the fine weather that they had had, as against Jane of last year. It was then a very cold month indeed, and as the past June had been more favourable he hoped that was the reason why there had been a decreased attendance this year. Alderman WEBSTER pointed out that the numbers were constantly affacted by circumstances entirely beyond their control. Sometimes they had something more attrac- tive than usual in the Library or Museum which attracted visitors—a greater numner than ordinary. But he thought if they considered the nice evenings the number would be found to be exceedingly satisfactory. When they saw that there were 601 persons who would go during the fine, warm, and beautiful weather and sit reading, neglecting, in a sense, the pleasures and beauties of the country, he did not think a decrease of 28 per cent was really much to de- plore. It wa3 very likely that next month they would see an increase—the attendance fluctuating in a way they could not account for. Alderman DaaaEs remarked that last year there was a decrease )vor the previous year, and it was evident there was a downvard course in the attendance. The MAYOR observed that they would find that when the attendance had been unusually great there had been some attraction—either pictures or something else—which had drawn large numbers to the Museum. The minutes were then carried. MISCELLANEOUS.
The minutes of the Witch, Finance, Paving and Sewer- age, and Getnetery Committees were passed without com- ment.
THE COST OF TEIE LONGFORD WORKS. BRANDY FOR SICK HORSES. ___ -

Alderman BURG'ESS moved and Councillor Moems seconded the confirmation of the proceedings of the Sani- tary Committee. Councillor MACKIE asked for information respecting the minutes of the Committee, and suggested that this Commit- tee also should have a menth to think upon the matter. Referring to a recommendation "That the Borough Surveyor and Mr. Dinwiddie report upon the present condition of the machinery and works at Longford, and prepare schemes, with plans and estimates, for putting into repair such machi- nery, akcerequired to treat the excreta upon the present steam drying principle, as also an alternative scheme upon the hot air system, to deal with 144 tens of excreta per week," the speaker said he really thought it was asking too much of them to pass a minute of that description seeing that upon these works so many thousands had been spent—without further informa- tion. One half the committee, he observed, had condemned the other half, and the whole coecem ought ere this to have been at the marine store dealers. (Laughter.) They would all be very glad to have the new machinery if they knew what kind it was to be, and if it would do its work; but he really thought it was treating the Council not in the way the Council treated the committee—which was with very great consideration—in asking them to pass the minute without giving a slight idea of the nature of the machinery —as to whether it came from Birmingham, Rochdale, Jericho, or where. (Laughter.) Deputations had been here, there, and everywhere with reference to this matter, and he was anxious that some scheme should be carried out which should be satisfactory ; but after what had been spent at Longford, they ought to know something more definite as to what was required before sanctioning the ex- penditure of more money. Councillor J. PIERPOINT endorsed the views of Councillor Dr. Mackie. Alderman HOLME9 pointed out that the committee were only asking for what the two previous speakers wanted. The committee asked their officials to prepare plans and specifications for the putting up of new machinery and the like. When these plans and specifications went before the committee the members would decide upon them in the affirmative or otherwise, and then their decision would come before the Council. The speaker went on to say that in looking over the financial statement of the Corporation for the past year he found that the absolute loss to the Corporation on the Longford works was £5,087, that was after receiving money for the manure and for everything sold; he also observed that that coin was an increase upon the previous year of something like £3OO. That £5,000 odd was an absolute charge upon the ratepayers of sd. in the S each half-year. He did not make these remarks with the view of fioding fault,because:the committee had to deal with circumstances of an exceedingly difficult nature ; but he did make them with the object of urging the committee that if they could by any means introduce into these works any machinery by which they could be carried on at a much less cost than in the past it was the duty of the com- mittee to do so, for 51 in the £ each half year was a serious charge upon the ratepayers. Councillor SUTTON : Is that 51. each half year? Alderman HOLMES : Yes. Councillor Surma; : Then it is 101 per year. Alderman HOLMES: Yes, between 101. and 11d. In the £ per year. Councillor WHITTLE observed that on pip 71 of the borough treasurer's report of the receipts and expenditure of the Corporation he found are item of £l3 Bs. for brandy for sick horses. (Laughter.) He thought they must have a drunken lot of horses—(renewed laughter)—and that the item required a little explanetion, for he knew people who employed as many horses as the Corporation, did, and they, did not spend as many shillings in drink on them. Alderman BURGESS, in replying to Councillors Mackie and Pierpoint, said the committee were not asking the Council for anything, but ouly to be furnished with in- formation from their officials, which, however, would lead up to something, and that would be the settling of the dif- ficult question regarding Longford—to determine what the machinery should be there, and to take a vote of the Council as to the outlay to be gone into on this matter. With re- ference to what Mr. Councillor Whittle had said, lie should t -committee, and he have to refer that gentleman to some other member of the scu7mnittee. The MAYOR, in moving the confirmation of the proceed- ings of the General Purposes Committee, drew attention to the recommendation "that the offer of a plot of land in Howley, containing 9,209 square yards, to be used as a pub- lic pleasure ground, at a rent of id. per yard per annum, be accepted." He said he was happy to tell the Council that the gentleman who had so generously offered this land at this low rate was their excellent townsman, Mr. Robert Davies. He (the Mayor) had mentioned to Mr. Davies the nutter of those open spaces, and told him %%hat Colonel Blackburne had done to secure a place in the north part of the town; and Mr. Davies said he had this land at Howley and he should he very glad indeed to do anything he could to assist the Corporation in providing open spaces for the use of children for all time to come. He wrote a very aice letter to the committee about it, and it gave him (the Mayor) very great pleasure to mention this in the Council Chamber that the people in Warrington might know that Mr. Robert Davies had offered this land at such a low rate. He (the Mayor) hoped this example would lead other owners of property to offer them other spaces of land on the same generous terms. Councillor BROADBENT seconded the motion. Councillor LITTON asked what foot bridge at Bank Quay the committee proposed to paint? The MAYOR: The one alongside the London and Nortk- Western railway. Councillor LITTON said that was railway property. The MAYOR s tid the bridge was the property of the Cor- por Won. who had made it.
Councillor WHITTLN asked how often the land at Howley was under flood?

The MAYOR: Once in five years, perhaps once in ten, and possibly once in 20 years. If once in five years, it would not do the ground any harm. Councillor SUTTON asked if in the purchase any restric- tions were imposed upon the Corperation as to the future use of the land supposing it failed as a pleasure resort. Could the Corporation under such circumstances use it for other purposes? Alderman DAVIES said there was a special Act of Parlia- ment under which these purchases or leases were made, and which provided that the land should be devoted to pleasure purposes only. Councillor Sumer said that the cost would be £4O a year, and if the land failed as a pleasure resort that would be simply so much loss to the Corporation. The MAYOR said it could not fail so long as there were any children in the town. Alderman BURGESS contended that open spaces, even if not used for the purpose spoken of, would still be invaluable to Warrington fur health's sake. But, as a matter of course, children should enjoy themselves, and the more there were of these places the. better. Where, he asked, was the plot of land situate? The MAYOR: Near Greenall-etrcet. It is bounded by Roberts, Dale and Co.'s works on one side. Alderman WEBSTER said he was pleased that the bpen spaces movement appeared to be 90 successful; but he should be still more pleased if some gentleman who had land to spare could see their way to let it out for gardening pur- poses for working people. In Nottingham he believed special plots were set apart for that purpose, and they were found to be beneficial to the health of the people who could work on the laud in their spare time. Something of that nature to be associated with the open spaces would, he thought, be of advantage, and would be appreciated. (Hear, hear.)

Alderman HOLMES moved, and Alderman WEBSTER seconded, the confirmation of the proceedings of tire GAS Committee. Councillor SUTTON drew attention to the following recom- mendation of the committee :—"That no gas stoves or other heating apparatus be let out in future on the hire system, but that the sale of them be purchase lease and absolute sele ha eocouraeed." He said the Chairman would perhaps explain to them why the recominendation was made, and whether it was to apply to those stoves or apparatus already let out on the hire system. It had always occurred to him (Councillor Sutton) that these gas stoves had been let out at a price which would not be remunerative, and perhaps that was the reason of the recommendation. Alderman EloeerEs said that so far as regarded the stoves let out on the hire system, there would be no alteration; but in the interest of the ratepayers and of the gas proprietors the committee thought it better to abandon the hire system for 'he future. Mr. Councillor Sutton must excuse him if he did not go further into the details. The committee had censidered the matter very carefully, and decided to adopt that course. They had now made arrangemenls to let these stoves out by annual rental, which they thought would recoup the committee the cost in three or five years. The minutes were adopted.

ALLEGED WRONGFUL SEIZURE OF PORK AT WARRINGTON. On Tuesday, at the Liverpool Assizes. before Mr: Justice Pearson and a special jury, the cause "Mynekyne v. The Mayor, &a., of Warrington and another," was heard. In this action John Mynekyne, pork butcher, Warrington, sought to recover eamages for malicious prosecution and wrongful conversion of his goods. The defendants; who were the Mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of Warrington, and Norman, their meat inspector, pleaded that they had reasonable and probable cause for what they did.—Mr. Walton and Mr. Nash, instructed by Mr. Percy Davies, were for the plaintiff, and Mr. Russell, Q.C., M.P., and Mr. But- ton, instructed by the Town Clerk, were for the defendants. Mr. Walton stated that the action was brought in respect of certain proceedings taken by the defendants against the plaintiff under the Public Health Act, 1875. The defend-. ant Norman seized certain pork which was upon the pre- mises of the plaintiff on the ground that it was unsound and unfit for food, and it was af•erwards destroyed as such by the order of a magistrate. The meat seized was the prin- cipal portion of a pig which had been purchased by the plaintiff on the 2nd February of this year. It was a boar pig, and the plaintiff bought it from a Mrs. Roughley. The animal weighed 3121 be., and the price which the plaintiff gave for it was £6. The learned counsel said he believed that was a fair price, and the size of the pig showed that it was not in an unhealthy condition. The pig was bought alive, and the plaintiff took it home to his premises where it remained until the Bth February, when it was killed. The carcase was hung up in the plaintiff's slaughter-house where the inspector vaw it on the following day. A portion of it was sold on the 10th, and the inspector saw it again on the 12th, but did not then say anything about it, and it was not until the 14th that the defendant thought it right to I seize the pork. Previous to its removal the plaintiff re- I tained one of the legs of the animal, which he submitted to the inspectors of meat in Liverpool, who declared that it was quite sound and that no honest man could believe there was anything wrong with it. The meat was also inspected by certain medical gentlemen after it was removed to the Town Hall, and they all declared that it was perfectly sound and in eriod condition. It was usual under the Public Health Act for the authorities to issue a summons against any who exposed unsound meat for sale, but the defendants found that they could not reasonably do this, and no sum- mons was issued. A ham of the pig was produced in court by the plaintiff, and it was shown that it was perfectly sweet and that one part of the pig could not be diseased and the other parts good. His Lordshio : Are you going to amne that this meat ap- peared to Mr. Norman to be fit for food,because the Act says "if it appears to him" to be unfit for food he may seize it? Mr. Walton: I am going to contend that it could not ob- viously appear to him to be unsound. His Lordship: Can you prove that? If the meat was so obviously sound the magistrates before whom it was taken would have ordered it to he returned to the plaintiff. It seems to me that the person who seized the meat had nothing to do with condemning it. Mr. Walton: He initiated the proceedings. His Lordship: Do you charge precedent malice between the two Mr. Walton: Well, it is difficult to put one's fingers upon strict evidence of that kind. His Lordship: It is not difficult if they have had a quarrel. Mr. Walton said he would show that the inspector had frequently within the last three or four years taken pro- ceedings against the plaintiff, and that all of these had fallen through. Mr. Russt ll said there were six cases, in all of which the magistrates ordered the meat to be destroyed. His Lordship siid he did not see how Mr. Walton was to make his case out against the defendants. Mr. Walton said he could prove a very good case as to the soundness of the pork. His Lordship: Assuming that you can, how are you to prove that it did not " appear " unsound to the in. ? Mr. Walton said that he could prove the thorough sound- ness of the meat, that no honest-minded man could have acted as the inspector had done, and that he should have to go on with the case. The plaintiff, Mr. Mynekyne, Mr. Ramsden (one of the largest butchers in Fngland), Mr. Luya and Mr. Tomlinson, meat inspectors of Liverpool, and Drs. Joseph, Jack, and Lip- trot, also spoke to having seen the meat, which they regarded as quite sound and fit for food, and the doctors also said that the meat had been very much illused by the inspector, and that it had been put in a pail with carbolic and urine and filth at the bottom For the defence it was contended that the meat was un- sound, and that there was reasonable and probable cause for what the defendants did. Dr. Gomel!, the medical officer of health for the borough of Warrington, said that he saw the meat at the plaintiff's shop. It was unsound, and quite unfit for food. He ordered the removal of the meat to the Town Hall.—Cross-examined by Mr. Nash: He could not tell why he did not give a cer- tificate for the meat to be destroyed, it was usual to give a certificate. Mr. Robrison, veterinary surgeon, also spoke to the meat being unfit for food and said that it was diseased—Cross- examined by Mr. Walton as to what disease it was suffering from, he said a "general stagnation" (which caused a general laugh in in court). By Mr. Walton: Could you not give a better definition of the disease than that.—No, he did not know that he could. Major Cartwright, the magistrate, also said that the pork was unsound and smelt dreadfully. The toremais of the jury hero intimated that the jury failed to see any case against the defendants. His Lordship said he quite agreed with the jury, and he believed that there was reasonable and probable cause for the magistrate to act as he did. He ordered a Yerdict and judg- ment for the defendants.

MISSIONARY MEETING AT THE EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL—The half-yearly meeting in connection with the Juvenile Missionary Association was held in the Brunswick Wesleyan Sunday School, Cross-lane, Earles- town, on Sunday afternoon last. There was a large attend- -1t1C,3 of teachers and scholars. The meeting was appro- priately opened by Mr. T. Newman, after which the energetic secretary, Mr. J. Profit, read the report, which though not quite as satisfactory as could have been desired, spoke hopefully for the future. He afterwards briefly ad- dressed the meeting, and was succeeded by the Rev. J. M. Fairbourn, who referred at some length to the hymn "From Greenland's icy mountains," and encouraged the children in their work of collecting. Mr. C. Atkinson also gave an ad- dress. Dative the course of the meeting the collectors, who had been efficiently trained, sweetly sang several appro- priate hymns; the meeting being concluded with singing And prayor.

A publican named Henry Moulds, residing at Colly Gate, who is alleged to have been drinking heavily for some time, went into a blacksmith's shop and hanged himself. Toe deceased weighed over twelve score. A CLERGYMAN FINED FOR BEING DRUNIL.—A.t Oxford, yesterday, the Rev. Nathaniel Cotton was fined 405., for being drunk and disorderly at fleadington. The rev, gentle- man denied the offence, and said he should appeal. THE REPORTED ASSASSINATION OF MOTTLEY.—A Dublin correspondent telegraphs that the safety of Mottley, the batter, is now ensured, and he is alive and well at Quebec. His reported assassination by Invincibles was therefore but a canard.

SiIoCKING OCCURRENCE AT HALESOWEN.—On Thursday night a shocking discovery took place at Jenkin's Farm, Halesowen. Upon a labourer putting a bowl into a wash cistern he brought up the dead body of his child, who had been missing several hours. Mr. John Bright has consented to open, on the 29th August, the Cobden Coffee-house, at Birmingham. Prior to the opening ceremony, the right hon. gentleman will be entertained at a luncheon by the Mayor and directors of. the Birmingham Coffee-house Company, and will sub3equently deliver an adlress in the Town Hall. FATAL SUBSIDENCE AT PORTSHOUTH.—WhiIe some men were engaged at Portsmouth yesterday on the demolition of the last section of the old ramparts which formerly sur- rounded Portsmouth, several tons of earth fell upon two labourers, one of whom was killed and the other bad his thigh broken. FATAL SHOOTING CASE —At Highgate, yesterday, Chas. Kent, 13, was remanded on bail, charged with causiog the death of Frederick Bunday, 18, gardener. While the de- ceased was at work on Thursday afternoon, a gun with which the defendant had been shooting went off suddenly, and the contents entered his head. The affair appeared quite acci- dental.

TRADE ORGANISATIONS AND INJURED WOREME'N. Hy. Dennis, a spinner employed by the Blackley Spinning Company, near Manchester, had his rigkt thumb taken off a short time ago. The Operative Cotton Spinners' Associa- tion, at their monthly meeting at Bolton, presented the dis- abled member with £lOO as compensation for the injury, which will permanently preclude him from following his employment. THE SCOTCH CROFTERS' COMMISSION STMIM-STAYED.—

During last night there was no abatement of tho gale on thel east coast of Scotland, and herring boats are yet missing. The gale raged with hurricane force on the west coast, and the North Star, with the Crofters' Commission on board, is lying storm-stayed at Mull, being unable to visit lona, where a sitting was fixed for yesterday. The storm has greatly damaged the potato crop in the Highlands. THE LOCKERBIE RAILWAY ACCIDENT: CLAIMS AGAINST THE COMPANY.—The railway accident that occurred at Lockerbie in May last promises to be attended by consider- able litigetion. By the friends of the killed and by the injured some heavy claims have been made against the Caledonian Railway Company. One or two of the claims are understood to be in a fair way towards settlement, but the others ate considered so exorbitant that the Railway Company decline to entertain them. THE WEATHER AT RLACEPOOL.—For two days there has been severe weather from the north-west at Blackpool. Yes erday the wind was very high, and rain fell in torrents. On Thursday afternoon aed evening the sea was most tem- p-stuous, the waves being sent over the promenade. The front, however, was not damaged. A large marquee in which a grand beztar was being held on behalf of Christ Church was rent in one part, and the wind getting in split up the tent in all directions. It collapsed in a heap on the ladies and gentlemen present, and most of the stalls were smashed. However, no person was injured and all were safely got out. , THE ABANDONMENT OF THE FARNELL DEMONSTRA- TION —The railway company offered to convey 2,000 ex- icursionists from Dublin on Sunday to the Parnell demon- stration at Avondale, but this accommodation was ' considered utterly inadequate. As m iny thousands besides that number would attend, the manager was unable to pro- vide rolling stock for the safe conveyance of the excur- sionists to such a remote place, and, to prevent accident arid loss of life, declined granting further facilities. The com- mittee charge the manager with breaking faith with them, and will publish the coirespondence between them. It is suggested that the demonstration should take place in the Phcenix Park, Dublin. A WOMAN IMPRISONED FOR ROBBING HER HUSBAND. —Yesterday, at Salford Police Court, Jane Delman, of 24, Cobbett-srreet, Salford, was charged under a warrant with stealing a silver lever watch, value £4, the property of her husband, Thomas Doleman. The case was brought under the Married Women's Property Act, 1882, and it was be- lieved it was the first of the kind which had been tried in that court. Evidence was then given to the effect that on Wednesday last the prisoner, who was of intemperate habits, went home the worse for drink, and she and her hus- band quarrelled, the latter stating that he would not "stand that sort of work" any longer. Upon this the prisoner said she would go, and went upstairs, put some articles in a bandbox, and went out. She called at the shop of a watch- maker, and obtained possession of her husband's watch, which had been left to be repaired. She subsequently pawned the watch.—Prisoner pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to one 1 month's imprisonment with hard labour.

div.head: CLOSE OF THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCF.
div.p: CLOSE OF THE WESLEYAN CONFERENCF.

At the Wesleyan Conference yesterday, foreign mission affairs, the Thanksgiving Fund, and temperance matters having passed under review, several motions of which notice had been given were discussed. The number of laymen allotted to the several distrjcts were announced, and the President delivered a closing address. The journal was then read and the usual votes of thanks were passed, and the Conference closed. DEATH OF DR. ROBERT MOFFATT.

The Press Association's Brighton correspondent says that a telegram was received yesterday morning by Mr. J. S. Unwin from MiS3 Moffatt, dated Leigh, Kent, stating that her father, Dr. Robert Moffattt, the celebrated African missionary and traveller, died on Thursday evening at half-past seven, lie was eighty-eight years old, and had been ailing for the past month. His health excited appre- hension, though be was able during the past week to take outdoor exercise.
THE DYNAMITE CONSPIRACY: ACQUITTAL
OF O'HERLIIIY.

At the Liverpool Assizes, yesterday morning, before Mr. Justice Stephen, Daniel O'Herlihy, who was acquitted by thedirection of the Judge of being concerned in the conspi- racy with the four men sentenced to penal servitude for life on Thursday, was brought up ou a charge of having with divers other persons conspired to murder some persons un- known. He pleaded not guilty, and no cvilence offered, he was acquitted and discharged from custody.
THE CHOLERA EPIDEMIC.
ALEXANDRIA, FRIDAY.
There were 22 fatal cases of cholera here during the 24 hours ending at 8 a.m. to-day. Most of the victims are natives. One death also occurred among the British troops at Ramleh.

In consequence of disturbances having occurred yesterday owing to the opposition of the natives to some measures of disinfection rendered necessary by a death through cholera in one of the native quarters, the Sanitary Commission have decided that a guard of Egyptian soldiers shall in future be present when such measures are carried out.

div.head: CIRCULAR BY LORD GRANVILLE
div.p: CIRCULAR BY LORD GRANVILLE

Among the parliam.mtary papers yesterday is a circular addressed by Lord Granville to British representatives abroani.ealing with the criticisms of Continental papers on the cholera, which, they allege, was introduced into Egypt from India throuoh the negligence of the British Govern- ment. Lord Granviile denies that the cholera was intro- duced from India, and points out that the English Govern- ment had refrained from Dressing any relaxation of the Suez quarantine regulations. The presence of British troops in Egypt should be a sufficient refutation of such ill- founded assertions.

Miss Arabella Kenealy bas received a letter from Lord Granville in reply to her offer to proceed to the seat of the cholera in Egypt, in which his lords Lip thanks Miss Kenealy for her offer, but points out that owing to the steady decrease of deaths there from the disease lately he does not think it rspediene to send out any more medical help from England, and must therefore decline her offer.

div.head: CHARGE OF INTIMIDATING JURORS.
div.p: THE CHARGE OF INTIMIDATING JURORS.

At the Liverpool Assizes, yesterday morninz, before Mr. Justice Stephen, the charges against Patrick O'Brien, coal dealer; Michael Hynes, printer; and Patrick Slater, com- positor, came up for hearing. The indictments charged that the prisoners "did, at Liverpool, on the 23rd April, 1883, maliciously c:mspire, combine, confederate, and agree, to- gether with other persons unknown, to obstruct, prevent, pervert, and defeat the course of public justice by printing, puJishing, and circulating certain documents relating to the service of certain persons on juries under the Crimes Act in Ireland ;" also that they did, "on the 13th May,

1883, maliciously write and publish a false, wicked, mali- cious, and scandalous libel of and concerning the adminis- tration of justice in this kingdom, and of and concerning the trial of certain persons under the Prevention of Crimes

(Ireland) Act, 1-882, and of and concerning the judges and jurors by whom the said trials were trial." [he indictment against O'Brien was first taken. Mr. J. A. Aspinall, QC., recorder of Liverpool, and Mr. Shand were counsel for the prosecution, and Dr. Commins, M.P., ap- peared for O'Brien.—Mr. Aspinall,Q C., in opening the case for the prosecution against O'Brien, said the prisoner at the bar had been charged with miademeanour in having pub- lished a libel on the administration of justice in Ireland. ' From counsel's further statement it appeared that the pri- soner had got printed at Hynes's place 10,000 copies of a list giving the names of the jurors who had .served on the Dublin trials with notes relating to individual jurors. These lists were posted at Manchester to people in Dublin, and en- closed in each envelope was a separate slip warning and threatening the receivers if they did business with the jurors on the list. The separate slip was not printed at Hynes's place, Evidence was given of the finding of the lists at Hynes's establishment and of their being sent through the tbe post-office. Dr. Commons addressed the jury for the defence, and the Judge summed up. The jury retired, and after an absence of live minutes returned in. to court with a verdict of guilty against O'Brien. The jury, in reply to the Judge, said they were of opinion that the prisoner published both slips—O'Brien was sentenced he six months' imprisonment; and Hynes and Slater were discharged.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS.—FRIDAY. Earl GRANVILLE, in reply to the Marquis of Salisbury, said that he had every reason to expect satisfactory con- clusions to the Madagascar affair, but it would not be politic that he should communicate the exact nature of the information.—The House then went into Committee on the Agricultural Holdings (England) Bill. On Clause 2 the Marquis of SALISBURY moved an amendment that there should be no compensation which vroald interfere with any specific agreement between the persons in reference thereto. —After discussion, the ameedment was carried by 116 to 46, and the clause was agreed to.—The Duke of RICHMOND moved an amendment to the effect that aeything due to the inherent capabilities of the soil not reckoned in the com- pensation to the tenant should apply to all improvements instead of to only those in parts one and two of the schedule. —The amendment was carried by 82 to 57. HOUSE OF COMMONS. ZULULAND.—Mr. ASHLEY, replying to Sir M. Beech, said it was impoesiole in the altered state of affairs in Zululand, and without knowing the objects of Cetewayo, to state at that time the course to be pursued regarding that country. THE BANKRUPTCY BILL.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said to- morrow he should propose that the Bankruptcy Bill be ex- tended to Ireland. If that was assented to, he hoped six members, who h'arl 255 amendments to the clauses, would not impede the progress of the bill. THE °runt TRADE.—Lord E. FITZMAURICE, replying to Mr. Richard, said negotiations were proceeding with China on the subject of opium. Certain proposals had been made by China, which her Majesty's Government under certain conditions were prepared to accept. THE CORRUPT PRACTICES BILL—The Corrupt Practices Bill was considered as amended.—Mr. GIBSON proposed, at the end of clause 8, to insert the following :—" Any person who before or deeing an election knowingly publishes any false statement of the withdrawal of a candidate at such election for the purpose of promoting or procuring the election of another candidate shall be guilty of an illegal practice."—After a discussion the words were added to the clause.—Mr. LABOUCHERE moved an addition to clause 15 to prevent the returning officer claiming more than the ex- penses allowed by the schedule.—The ATTORNEY-GENERAL objected to the addition, as he thought it hard to prevent the returning officer—if be had Spent £5O beyond the ex- penses allowed and the candidate was agreeable to repay it —receiving the monev.—Sir R. CROSS supported the addi- tion to the clause, and a discussion ensued.—Sir H. Holland, H. Fowler, and-others supported the addition to the clause. —On a discussion there voted for it 71, and against 93. On clause 16 Mr. BEALY proposed an addition to the clause, providing that every bill posted or placard issued during an election should bear the name and • address of the printer, and also the name and address of the candi- date, or the person by whom it was issued; and that non- compliance with the provision should be deemed an illegal practice, and subject the offender to a flue of £loo.—The addition wrs agreed to.—An amendment by Lord G. HAmeLyore, making further protection as to places to be hired as committee-rooms, was agreed to. In clause 21, which made provision for the nomination of election agents, a number of verbal amendments were moved by 'Mr. HEALY and agreed to —Other amendments were also made in several clauses.—ln clause 37, which provided for the withdrawal of election petitions, Mr. RAIKES moved an amendment giving the Director of Public Prose- cutions; the power of examining persons on oath, whose evi- dence the Public Prosecutor cmsidered material.—The ATTORNEY GENERAL opposed, and the amendment was rejected by 100 to 21.—The sitting was then suspended.

div.head: VIADUCT WORKS EXCURSION
div.p: THE VIADUCT WORKS EXCURSION
TO LONDON.
A LONDON BITER BITTEN.

A correspondent writes :--It ruay not be generally known that within your district an extensive trip to London has just been made, patronised principally by railway employis. One incident connected therewith is worth recording, show- ing, as it does, that occasionally a man from the country unaccustomed to "city professionalism " proves himself fit to leave his native sod. The individual alluded to has al— ways been considered .scarcely up to par (to use a county phrase) in his top garret, and learning that he intended joining the excursion his comrades thought it wise to warn him of the many " traps " with which the great metropolis abounds. He was specially cautioned against the pickpocket, who, if he was not careful, they said would relieve him of his purse. To such advice he appar- ently took little heed, though from what transpired it is evident it was not without its influence upon him. Quietly, and unknown to his friends, he hit upon an original safe.- guard. Previous to commencing the journey he made a purchase—two pennyworth of fish-hooks. With these he carefully lined his trousers pocks freely, planting them all hook downwards. The train arrived at London, and amongst the excursionists was the man who had previously been designated " %mit headed." Our country friend, however, sauntered out of the station, and gazed about the thronged street and at the busy multitude. Presently his eye caught sight of a crowd, whither be was at once at- tracted. Almost instantly he discovered someone's hand in his pockets. Having every confilence in the efficacy of his plan he was in no ways anxious about his purse. Presently he moved away, and of course the "sharper" was obliged to follow, though the man from the country never appeared to, be cognisant of his presence. Seeing the state of things a gentleman made up to cur country friend and said, "I say my man, this fellow has his hand in your pocket." In the coolest manner imaginable came the reply, "Well, ler him ger it eawt." Knowing he was caught, and having a regard for his tortured fingers, the would-be pickpocket implored forgive- ness and nagged to be released from his painful and uncom- fortable position. Being of a generous turn of mind, the country excursionist agreed to let the fellow off for the modest sum of sixpence—the cost of the fish hooks and a new pocket—And at once commenced the operation of cut- ting away his pocket. The London sharper's agony provided fun for the group who witnessed his capture, and on once getting free he was soon out of his sight. The united opinion of the countryman's friends is "that be is not so green as be is cabbage looking," an old proverb in which the London pickpocket doubtless fully concurs.

It was decided that the first taam should wear new jerseys—blue awl white quartered and that Tuesday and Thursday nights should he the practice nights for the future. The meeting concluded with a vote of thanks to the chairman,

SUICIDE OF A CONVICT.—David Mackie, machinist, who was sentenced last week to ten years' penal servitude for the attempted murder of his wife at Birmingham, committed suicide in Warwick Gaol on Tuesday by hanging himself in his cell.
